speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It relates to the Monday, May 30, 1960 edition of the Hamilton Spectator and an editorial that appears on page 6 of that edition. The heading of that editorial is "A One-Man Defiance of Parliament". If I may, I should like to read one sentence from it. This has reference to Senate private bills relating to divorce. It states:
They are being blocked now to satisfy the declared ulterior motive of one C.C.F. member of parliament, Frank Howard of Skeena.

subtopic: MR. HOWARD    REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN HAMILTON "SPECTATOR"
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. HOWARD    REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN HAMILTON "SPECTATOR"
speechtext:
Regardless of the applause, apparently for the editor, may I point out that this is absolutely untrue and that there are no ulterior motives. The motives have been stated time and again; they are open and declared, and are not hidden, unethical and secret as this editorial indicates. Another sentence, referring again to myself, says:
Now he has openly threatened that he will hold up all the bills until the government changes the system or, in other words, forces divorce courts on the two provinces.
This also, Mr. Speaker, is untrue and nothing short of editorial falsehood. The entire editorial, and I do not want to read it all, is full of inaccuracies and I think represents how far out of touch with the times the editor of this paper is. If it wanted to be full and factual the editorial should have made reference not only to myself but also to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) who is also participating in this sort of debate. It should also refer to the silent approbation and commendation which I have received from other hon. members-

speechtext: Order. The hon. member has risen to express a question of privilege, not to indicate what might have been said otherwise. I take it the point is that objection is taken to the reference in the editorial to ulterior motives.

subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON ADMISSION OF ADDITIONAL REFUGEES

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON ADMISSION OF ADDITIONAL REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief announcement concerning the implementation of the extension I announced in the house last March of the government project for the admission to Canada of additional tuberculosis refugees and their families.
Hon. members will recall that under the original scheme last winter 100 t.b. cases and their families, comprising a total of 344 persons, were brought to Canada. The selection and processing of the refugees to be admitted under the extension is at present being carried out by our immigration officers stationed in Germany, Austria and Italy. The provincial governments have given us every co-operation in this project, and as a result of the undertakings they have given in connection with the extension it will be possible to place at least 100 additional t.b. cases, and possibly more, in the provincially operated sanatoria.
The stage has now been reached where it has been possible to make definite arrangements to bring the first group of t.b. cases and their families to Canada in chartered aircraft which will leave Europe on July 18 and July 25. If the processing of the third group of refugee families can be completed in time they will be flown to Canada in a charter aircraft leaving Europe on August 1.
Although the selection process has not been completed, reports which have been received so far indicate that somewhat broader categories of refugees will be available for inclusion in the extension than were included in the original 100 family scheme. It appears probable, for example, that some unmarried refugees suffering from t.b. may be admitted, as well as a number of refugees who have relatives already residing in Canada. It is also possible that families with more than one t.b. case will be included in the movement.

Inquiries of the Ministry
I am sure all hon. members will welcome the news that the first of these unfortunate refugees to benefit from the extension will be arriving in Canada in a very few weeks to begin building a new life.

subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON ADMISSION OF ADDITIONAL REFUGEES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON ADMISSION OF ADDITIONAL REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the applause indicates the feeling not merely of the house but of the country that what the government is doing in extending this scheme is a very good thing. So far as we are concerned we are in complete support of what is being done. Our only conceivable criticism is that perhaps it is a little on the small side.
I would like at this time to make an appeal to the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Green) to hasten the decision on the submission of the Canadian welfare council with respect to health and welfare care of privately sponsored refugees so we can get good results from private sponsorship, which is very difficult as long as this eternal liability is going to be placed on them.

subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON ADMISSION OF ADDITIONAL REFUGEES
speechtext: This group gives wholehearted support to the government's action in this direction, which we take to be a tangible expression of Canadian support for humanitarian principles and sympathies.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether the Canadian government has been yet officially informed of Mr. Khrushchev's latest disarmament proposal. If so, has he any comment he would care to make about it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had word from our ambassador in Moscow that he was called in yesterday by Mr. Gromyko and handed a personal letter for the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) from Mr. Khrushchev, enclosing a rather lengthy document on disarmament. The full text of the document is not yet available to me. However, from the brief summary I have seen it appears that the document contains the details of the new proposals which Mr. Khrushchev announced a few hours later at his press conference.
The house will realize that it is not possible for me to comment on the proposals at this moment, but this communication from the Soviet government will have to be carefully considered by the government before a reply could be made.
I will say this, Mr. Speaker; that it is obvious from the nature of the statement that it is quite heavily weighted for propaganda purposes. Mind you, in saying that I would not wish to leave the impression that the proposals will not be given the most careful consideration. However, the 10-nation committee on disarmament is resuming
Inquiries of the Ministry its sittings on Tuesday next, and this will be a very good opportunity for the Soviets and their associates to put forward this proposal for consideration. There have also been proposals put forward to that committee by the five western nations.
It seems to me that there are two main courses open to this committee. One is to analyse all these different proposals in an earnest and sincere attempts to reach some agreement. This, of course, is the course which the Canadian delegation will endeavour to see is followed in the committee by all parties concerned, the representatives from both east and west. The other course could be to use the sittings of the committee for propaganda purposes and for building up a case to be argued out at the meeting of the general assembly of the United Nations which commences, I think, on September 20. I am very hopeful that this second course will not be followed, although there are suggestions that this attempt might be made. It does seem to the Canadian government that a course of that type would be very unfortunate and certainly would not be very helpful to the cause of disarmament or of world peace.
There is one feature that I should like to place before the house today. That is that in spite of the failure of the summit conference, the cold war in all its fury has not been resumed as yet as many feared would be the case. There seems to be a desire on the part of those involved to keep tension relaxed as much as possible. I am hoping some worth-while results will flow from the meetings of the disarmament committee which will commence so soon.
Canada has suggested to her fellow members from the west that meetings should not all be of a public nature, but that from time to time there should be private meetings with only the heads of delegation present and which would not be subject to full reports to the press. The practice so far has been to keep full records of the meetings, and while the reports are not given out at once they are published after a matter of a few weeks' time.
As hon. members will realize from their own personal experience in the House of Commons, this constitutes quite a temptation to talk for the record. The Canadian delegation believes there should be at last some private meetings when real negotiations can take place, and when those speaking do not have to worry about what their words are going to look like when published a few weeks later.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):

speechtext:
I have some information today, Mr. Speaker. I noted an article which


appeared in this morning's Globe and Mail somewhat similar to what the hon. member for Ottawa West has said, to this effect:
John Profumo, British minister of state for foreign affairs, declared here that his government was ready to consider joining the European atomic energy agency and the European coal and steel community.
The hon. member's question was somewhat similar, to this effect:
In view of the announcement this morning by the United Kingdom in Paris that she is prepared to join the European coal and steel community and EURATOM, can the minister advise the house whether or not Canada was advised of this action prior to the announcement being made and whether or not it involves any change in our preferential position in the United Kingdom market?
There seems to be a misunderstanding here. No declaration to that effect was made by Mr. Profumo, I am informed. He was in attendance at the assembly of the western European union in Paris on June 2. The assembly had before it a draft recommendation concerning the possibility that the United Kingdom might join EURATOM. I have not seen the actual text of Mr. Profumo's statement, but I am informed that he said the United Kingdom would be prepared to look again at the possibility of joining EURATOM and the European coal and steel community. It has not gone further than a statement that he would have another look at a proposal that had been before the assembly on a previous occasion.
On the point of consultation with Canada, I have no doubt at all but that consultation will take place, that is prior to any step by the United Kingdom. We have been closely in touch with the proposals affecting the Six and the Seven, and it is inconceivable that they would take any action without letting us know what they were contemplating before that action was taken.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a supplementary question to the minister. Has there been consultation between the two governments on this particular proposal?

speechtext: No, because this proposal was not made by Mr. Profumo at all; it originated, I am given to understand, in that assembly from other sources.

499. Purchase and transportation to Chile of flour and pork for the relief of Chilean disaster victims and to authorize reimbursement of the agricultural commodities stabilization account in respect of the purchase of such pork, $1,600,000.
I realize that the notice to the members of the committee is extremely short, but in

Supply-External Affairs view of the great urgency of the matter may I ask whether the committee might be prepared to take this item first, to pass it, report the item, then permit the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means in order to deal with the corresponding resolution in committee of ways and means, have it reported and allow the bill to be given at least first reading today.

We simply have nothing in the estimates covering this matter. It is an unexpected calamity. In view of the urgency I would ask the committee to give its consent. I have had the opportunity to speak to hon. members opposite and I believe this course will be supported by them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
In so far as notice is concerned, we on this side of the chamber do not consider it necessary under these circumstances, and we are prepared to give full support to this measure. I think the committee will be happy with the decision of the government to come to the assistance of these people in Chile who have suffered so much because of the tragedy that has befallen them.
The decision the government has taken to give assistance to Chileans in this form is one, of course, which the government is in a far better position to determine than are the members of the opposition. Whether this form or some other form is better it seems to me is a matter for the government to decide, and with that we can find no fault. We do think that if there is going to be assistance, if it is the intention of parliament to grant assistance to those who have suffered, it should be given to them immediately and without any delay.
With that in mind we support this item for immediate approval.

Mr. Chairman, this group gives complete endorsement of this further action on the part of the government to assist disaster-stricken Chile. We recognize the need for haste. We are all in favour of getting this assistance into the hands of the people who need it as soon as possible, and on that account we are willing to co-operate in any way we can to pass the various stages of necessary legislation as expeditiously as possible.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I thank the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Kootenay West for their support of this item. Fortunately it was possible for me to learn from the minister of the interior of Chile direct what type of assistance he would prefer from Canada, and the provision of the flour and the canned meat are two of the items he requested.
I had a wire just a few minutes ago from our ambassador to Chile, Paul Tremblay, who is doing an outstanding job, by the way, reporting on a visit he had paid to the stricken area. This wire will give hon. members some idea of just what is going on in that country which has suffered such a blow. He says:
I have just returned from a few hours visit to Puerto Montt where our two North Stars flew in their supplies and brought back evacuees (including two stretcher cases) yesterday. General impression is that of a city accurately and selectively bombed but where no major fire developed. Three successive earthquakes and abnormal ten foot tide on May 21 and 22 left 147 dead destroyed 50 per cent of the houses mostly in poor districts. There are some 25,000 homeless and downtown streets are flooded. Due to destruction of water mains and sewage system main hotel had to be evacuated. The hospital police headquarters a flour mill and cheese factory a food packing plant are now so many heaps of rubble. Puerto Montt has 45,000 population is end of railway line to south and is the supply centre for the whole southern region of Chile. Its excellent harbour facilities have now been wrecked. Water front has apparently sunk two metres at places concrete wharves are broken or tumbled and frogmen are endeavouring to recover cranes and other equipment. Railway station nearby badly damaged and re-establishment of railway communication will take at least two months. Local needs are for tents clothing blankets for homeless. Medical supplies in Puerto Montt are now adequate. I was told food supplies are available for immediate needs in Puerto Montt city hall and other distribution centres. Hundreds of people queueing for emergency relief. A local requirement is for tarpaulin or waterproof plastic material to protect flour vegetables fruits etc from rain. The Canadian Red Cross representatives here will report on general requirements directly to their headquarter after tour of the disaster area.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to pay tribute to the Canadian Red Cross for the help they have given. In addition they have sent representatives to Chile. The telegram continues:
I was received by governor of province and military authorities who were almost embarrassingly profuse in expressing their appreciation and gratefulness for assistance provided by Canadian Red Cross and Canadian government. Governor is also responsible for island of Chiloe where Ancud and Castro are located. He said that our hospital unit in Castro will fill urgent need. Local hospital was wrecked and flooded and although number of wounded is not large there are large number of cold exposure cases particularly children infection pneumonia etc. Our unit will also take care of people from Ancud thus providing independent medical facilities for the island.

We left our equipment safely stored in Puerto Montt and as soon as tent arrives tomorrow hospital unit will be flown from Puerto Montt by small aircraft and helicopter to Castro. My general impression shared by Canadian Red Cross representatives is that relief organization in Puerto Montt is working smoothly with assistance of police and military reinforcement sent from Santiago.
That will give the committee a pretty clear picture of just what is going on in that country.

It would be surprising if when we were discussing the estimates of the Department of Transport some comment did not come from this quarter with respect to the gem of the national harbours board, the port of Vancouver. Many of my remarks will be complimentary to the minister and his officials, for after many long years of neglect and disregard this great port facility is receiving, certainly in the initial phase, some of the attention it so rightly deserves.
I am sure the minister was as pleased as I was to find that according to the 1959 report, during the past year 60 per cent of the arrivals and departures of vessels at all the national harbours board ports in Canada, and 40 per cent of the gross tonnages and almost 30 per cent of all the cargo, used this great facility; a facility which, I again point out, has so far cost the people of Canada nothing. It operated again at a profit of well over $1 million, and this after a year when at long last the national harbours board decided to spend an amount more in keeping with the requirements for the maintenance of the port. Spending in connection with these needs was raised at last to something considerably greater than was spent on the port of Churchill, with 132 vessels moving in and out each year, compared with almost 30,000 vessels moving in and 30,000 vessels moving out of the port of Vancouver in the calendar year.

Supply-Transport
I mention these points just in order that the committee may have some idea of the importance and the urgency of the problem concerning this great facility which has grown up through years of disregard and neglect. The minister announced in the house on June 12 last the establishment of an interdepartmental study to consider the development program required by the port of Vancouver. Shortly thereafter this interdepartmental body was brought into being and began its work. At the same time certain measures were taken to study the terminal rail facilities Which today still remain in a state of utter confusion, with a complex pattern of arbitrary and unjust switching charges which operate against the economy of the whole of western Canada and the future usefulness of the port itself.
I should like to tell the minister how pleased and enthusiastic the people of the west coast were to learn that these studies would be undertaken. But I hasten to warn the minister that after 12 months these urgent matters should be the subject of a report, as the interdepartmental study should consist basically only of the groundwork in preparation for a fuller and broader study in which industry, commerce, the carriers and the municipalities affected by the development of these facilities may have an opportunity to submit their just case and worth-while suggestions. I say to the minister that if his estimates are to be greeted again-if the national harbours board vote is to be greeted again-with pleasure by those of us who come from the west coast, it will only be so if these studies are kept on the urgent, active basis so urgently required.
During the past year there has been a notable development which has further emphasized the shortcomings of the facilities available at the port. The Pacific and Orient Lines have announced the introduction of a very extensive trans-Pacific passenger vessel service. This is a matter of great concern to us. Now we find that the Pacific and Orient Lines will be wishing in less than a year to berth passenger vessels of 40,000 tons or more, vessels much larger than those which normally have made use of our port. There are no terminal facilities whatever capable of handling or properly berthing vessels of this size. This again is a reflection on the past, when this gem of the national harbours board ports of Canada was disregarded with complete indifference to the needs of the Pacific coast region. The development to which I have referred emphasizes the need for providing terminal passenger facilities in line with those which have been available

in every other national harbours board port for many years but which are denied the port of Vancouver.
All this brings me to the point of taking a look at a skelton in the closet. I wish to bring it forth and talk about it. This is a matter which has concerned me greatly. Governments in the past have chosen to leave this thing in hiding. I have endeavoured to discuss the matter with officials of the national harbours board but they have looked askance, perhaps not unreasonably, because I am sure it involves a matter of policy the solution to which rests in the minister's hands. I refer to the clouded title to the right of way running along the water lanes and the water frontage now occupied by the Canadian Pacific railway, along the south of Burrard inlet. I am not saying that I join with any of those who say that title to this property does not belong to the C.P.R., nor am I one who says it does not belong to the crown. I am here to say on these estimates that it is time the national harbours board took a stand on the matter.
The matter should be brought to the courts to find out where the title truly rests, because the eventual proper utilization of the port, its proper planning and its value to the people of this nation, depend upon who controls the title.
We were just discussing the need for terminal passenger facilities, and I mentioned the need for an entirely new approach to the problem of terminal rail facilities. The title to this property holds the key to the way this problem can be approached, ft is my view that the national harbours board should seek through the courts at the earliest possible time a decision that will dispel the existing cloud with reference to this title and clear the way to solve this urgent need for passenger facilities.
If the title to these properties rests properly in the hands of the C.P.R. the future action is clear. We, the government of Canada, must see that the C.P.R. creates the necessary facilities on those lands. If they refuse to do so, and they do hold title to these properties, then the next thing is to demand that the government expropriate the property and enter into the construction of the facilities that are so desperately needed. If, on the other hand, the title rests with the federal government, the issue is clear. It is up to the national harbours board to act and provide the necessary passenger terminal facilities.
While discussing matters relating to the national harbours board I should like to say a brief word about bridges. We have heard a great deal of discussion in this chamber and elsewhere regarding the current spending, the

past spending and the proposed future spending on bridges across navigable waters in the Montreal area. We on the west coast have bridge problems. We have many major multimillion dollar bridges crossing navigable waters in that area, including the first narrows bridge at the entrance to Burrard inlet, the two bridges at the second narrows, the Oak street bridge, the Granville street bridge and the Patullo bridge and others on the Fraser river.
Supply-Transport
for leadership in the department, and if the proper leadership does not correct this problem of immobility, inefficiency and waste then it needs a thorough housecleaning. In this instance we have witnessed immobility on the part of a bureaucratic organization chasing itself around in wild circles until I think it will vanish off the face of the earth. It has cost us thousands of dollars and has produced nothing of value for the people of Canada.
The cost of these has been borne by the people of British Columbia. We can go to Halifax or Quebec city or elsewhere in Canada and find that the approach or policy with reference to bridges differs from that applying in Montreal. I submit that there is no policy with respect to bridges on the west coast, and I submit that Canada must have a policy applicable to bridges crossing navigable waters generally. Either we must estab-lsh a bridge policy that will meet the problem and ensure that bridges are provided and properly maintained, or we should get out of the bridge business entirely. It is urgent that the bridge policy be unified across this nation.
Last year a tragic marine disaster occurred just off the shores of my constituency. It is widely known as the Ferngulf disaster. As a result of that tragedy the minister undertook a study and made an announcement regarding the establishment of a new coastal marine service. The people of the west coast, and I am sure the people of coastal areas elsewhere in Canada, were pleased about that announcement, but today they want clarification. They would like some details of the operation and a report on what is being done. This service must be brought into existence. Like the whole question of the port of Vancouver it is a matter of great urgency.
I wish now to deal briefly with the subject of airports. In this connection I regret that I cannot extend congratulations to the minister and his department when I reflect on the absolutely amazing sequence of events that has occurred concerning the Myrtle Point airport at Powell River. It would be the only such facility on the upper coastal mainland provided in a fog-free area to protect against emergencies should the lower mainland of greater Vancouver be fogbound.
In my efforts to get to the bottom of this matter-and I have consistently worked at it on a weekly basis for many months-I have developed that strange, frustrated feeling of a swimmer trying to go up the Fraser river against the incredible currents that abound there. Today we have reached the appalling stage where officialdom is calling on the town of Powell River to help finance a program announced two years ago by the federal government without any discussion at that time with the municipal authority. I have been unable to obtain adequate information on this matter, and I bring it once again to the attention of the minister, not as a means of criticizing him but as a means of stressing the urgent need that a serious look be taken at this branch of an otherwise efficient department.
I wish to thank the committee for the opportunity of reviewing these matters. I wish the minister continued success this year

I wish now to deal with some local problems of interest to everyone along the coast of British Columbia. The Simon Fraser is a buoy and supply vessel costing in the neighbourhood of $3 million which replaced the old Alberni and was to be based at Prince Rupert in fulfilment of a promise made by the federal government. The problem is Prince Rupert versus Victoria, as it were. It is true that this promise was made during the time the Liberal government was in office,

Supply-Transport
but it is still a commitment that should have been kept with the people of Prince Rupert and with the communities and areas and lighthouses which would have been serviced by the Simon Fraser out of Prince Rupert.
Until about a month or so ago the only vessel that was stationed there was the old, inadequate, antiquated Alexander Mackenzie. Beyond that there was nothing in the line of ships of this type to service the area. This has meant at the economic end that perhaps 20 or so families who had been living in Prince Rupert have had to tear up their roots, as it were, and leave. Now that the Alberni is gone and the Simon Fraser is to be stationed some 500 or 600 miles away in Victoria, this is the situation.
In the past Prince Rupert has not looked too kindly upon federal governments. Probably the worst betrayal they experienced in recent years was the sale and removal of the drydock at Prince Rupert. This was done under a Liberal administration. It was something which upset the residents of Prince Rupert and the economy there to no end. If the attitude of the present government or of the minister with respect to the Simon Fraser is to continue the people in Prince Rupert will develop, if they have not already developed, the same attitude toward the Conservative government that they had toward the Liberal government when the drydock there was cut up into little pieces, uprooted and sold to somebody who not only took it away from Prince Rupert but out of the country entirely.
I understand the Simon Fraser is being based in Victoria. This is in line with what the minister or his officials term a need for greater flexibility in the use of those particular vessels.
We have a great need on the west coast, as they do on the east coast, for some sort of coastguard arrangement which would be far better than what we have had in the past. This is particularly true in the case of a ship disaster. The north coastal waters, the area of Hecate strait and the entrances around the Queen Charlotte islands and Prince Rupert get extremely violent at times, because they border on waters which are open to the Pacific. If there are disasters there we shall again have to rely upon United States coastguard facilities to effect any rescue. Apart from that, the Alexander Mackenzie is considered, as I mentioned earlier, to be an antiquated or inadequate type of vessel for servicing lighthouses, replacing buoys and other navigational aids. In servicing lighthouses with supplies, especially when they are perishable goods, there is some doubt as to whether those supplies can get there

in the condition in which they should be when they arrive; that is, if they are frozen, whether they will remain in that condition and not deteriorate.
The minister was in Prince Rupert in the summer of 1957; I forget the exact date, but it would be around July or August. It was after the federal election of 1957, in any event. He spent a day or so there. He had occasion to tour the city and spend a period of time on the Alberni itself with officials of the Department of Transport and the city of Prince Rupert. He toured the construction work that was then taking place on the new airport at Prince Rupert. Although I had occasion to meet the minister for only a few moments while he was there I would assume that during the time he and his staff were there he had occasion to get a fairly complete picture of the economic and geographic circumstances surrounding Prince Rupert. I am sure in his own mind he knows and appreciates those problems to the fullest extent by reason of his visit there, and certainly by reason of subsequent reports that he has undoubtedly received since that time.
If the minister needs any refreshing of his memory as to the great need-I refer now to the Simon Fraser-for the establishment of this vessel at Prince Rupert, then I am quite sure he would find that the entire city would again welcome him with open arms as they did then. He could then reinforce his memory about the need for this particular vessel to be stationed there rather than in the capital city of Victoria, which is some 500 or 600 miles south.
I am in no position to extend any official invitation on behalf of the city of Prince Rupert, but I know members of the city council, members of the chamber of commerce and other organizations in Prince Rupert, and I know the minister would be most welcome at any time, and especially now. Our people would be happy to remind him of the great need that exists in Prince Rupert for the establishment of this particular vessel there rather than in Victoria down at the southern end of Vancouver island. Perhaps this is what the minister needs, a sort of west coast, two or three week vacation from his arduous task of running probably the largest department in the government. It would not only assist him but would be beneficial and give him a psychological rest from his chores and duties. I am sure it would assist his memory and understanding of the requirements of that particular part of the country, and it might even be beneficial in getting the minister to change his mind and place the Simon Fraser in Prince Rupert, where it was promised she would be and where she should be rather than in Victoria, where she would be of

relatively little value to the upcoast except on the occasional visit she makes there in her tours.
I should also like to make a comment or two about the airport at Prince Rupert. This is a pretty sore point. It was a sore point with the city of Prince Rupert and the people there during the past winter as it was during the winter of 1958-59. We all know, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Transport's colleague, the Minister of Labour, has been engaged in the last two years on what he classifies as an extensive winter works program to encourage municipalities to undertake certain types of work in the winter period to ease unemployment. At the same time the Minister of Labour has been pushing this particular program of winter works with the municipalities to ease unemployment, the Minister of Transport has been working in the opposite direction by curtailing work which could have been carried on in winter time on the airport itself.
This is not a question that was raised just this past winter. As I mentioned, there was concern felt all during the winter of 1958-59, and there was hope that some extensive examination could take place. The people of the city of Prince Rupert could see far enough into the future, if the minister could not, to see what would occur during the past winter of 1959-60. There were statements many months ago concerning the need for work on that airport during the winter months which would not only speed up completion of the airport but would also ease the unemployment situation in Prince Rupert. It seems that on the one hand we have the Minister of Labour proposing and pushing a particular scheme to ease unemployment, and on the other hand his colleague the Minister of Transport holding back, delaying and procrastinating on the very same thing.
I do not need to refer again to the fact that the minister was out there in 1957 and toured the airport work. He has knowledge of it from a personal inspection as well as from reports. I say again, if he would like to return at any time to refresh his memory concerning the need that exists, although the winter has passed, he would still be welcome. There has been some extensive correspondence in this connection, and the minister was kind enough to send me a copy of a letter which he sent to His Worship Mayor Lester of the city of Prince Rupert. The letter is dated February 15, 1960 and sets out in some detail the work which is still to be done on the airport and the dates upon which this work would be expected to be commenced.

Perhaps I might be permitted to make a brief reference to the letter itself, Mr. Chairman, without reading it in its entirety, although if anyone so desires certainly it is easy enough to place the letter on record so the full intent of the minister will be seen. He makes reference to the air terminal building, and indicates that plans and specifications for that building are in an advanced stage of preparation, and so on. However, he says it may well be that the construction period will be in excess of 12 months from the time of the award of the contract. This really does not meet the great need that exists for the completion of that airstrip. The people of Prince Rupert are not concerned about activities 12 months hence.
At the time the letter was written by the mayor-incidentally, it was written on December 7 of last year-he was concerned about an immediate start on the construction in order to complete the airport and also provide employment to ease the unemployment situation. All he got in reply was that something might occur 12 months from then, or that after the contract was awarded the building might be completed within 12 months. The minister also makes reference to the I.L.S., the radio buildings and emergency power and says it is expected that tenders will be called within two or three weeks of the date of this letter. The target date for commissioning is September 30, 1960. This is not the period of time within which the work would have been most beneficial, and in keeping with the expressed aims of this government.
In so far as power service to the airport is concerned, the runway and approach lighting, it is expected that tenders will be called for this work in March, 1960, with the target for completion August 31, 1960. Then there is the clearing for the hazard beacon. The indication was that tenders had been called for that project as of the date of the letter, and it was expected the work would be completed entirely within the winter months, which was the initial request of the city of Prince Rupert.
In so far as the equipment garage is concerned, the indication here is that this purchase would be completed within the next few weeks. This is a small part of the total work involved, but it would also have been completed within the period. As I say, it is too late now because winter is over, and this project cannot be made part of the government's winter works program to try to ease unemployment, which I think should have been done. Nevertheless, I raise the matter as a sort of complaint of past failures.
I should like now to make brief reference on this transport question to the proposed

Supply-Transport
railway to be constructed in the interests of the Wenner-Gren foundation. It is proposed
to build the line from somewhere near Prince George north to the British Columbia-Yukon border and, perhaps later on, through the Yukon Territory to Alaska. This, Mr. Chairman, is part of the sell-out by our provincial government in British Columbia to the Wenner-Gren interests, a part of the steal of one tenth of the province of British Columbia. At the moment we have in that particular area two railways; one is the Canadian National northern line that runs through Jasper and Prince Rupert, and the other is the Pacific Great Eastern Railway which runs from North Vancouver up through Prince George and thence farther north. I am only concerned with the Prince George section at the moment. The proposal of the Wenner-Gren people is that an additional railroad should be constructed starting somewhere near Prince George-I am not thoroughly familiar with the exact take-off point-and going in a sort of northwesterly direction along the Rocky mountain trench up to the Yukon border.
I really believe this proposal for the construction of this railroad has more connection with an expected provincial election in British Columbia than it has with anything else. If they think they are just going to build a railroad that is going to stop at the Yukon border in the north, then this company and the provincial government are a bit nuts. Logically this should be a railroad that runs up to Alaska, and to that extent the federal government is involved, the Department of Transport is involved and perhaps the Canadian National Railways, even though apparently they do not want to be involved, because the railway would then be outside the province of British Columbia and would come under federal jurisdiction.
The proposed route of the railroad, as the minister will know, is in the wrong place. It is not economically feasible and it is not sensible to build it from its present take-off point. I submit that if the Canadian National is not going to participate, and apparently they are not, the railway should start from Hazelton, thence northward along a fairly decent route to whatever the terminus would be in the north. This was called route A. It was seriously considered by the United States defence department as an alternate route to Alaska during the second world war, that is an alternate route to the present Alcan highway. So far as I know, the route has been completely topographically surveyed by the provincial department of lands and forests as far back as six or eight years ago.
I understand that the president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Gordon, has

written to Premier Bennett on two occasions making some suggestions with respect to this proposed railway the provincial government is sponsoring. He has suggested that the Wenner-Gren people use that part of the Canadian National Railway right of way from Prince George west to Hazelton and then go northward from there. It is pointed out that this would save approximately $30 million which otherwise would be spent for that some 200 or more miles of heavy construction that would have to be done for the Wenner-Gren railway. It is quite a logical suggestion and one that should be accepted, in my opinion, because the two railways-that is the Canadian National Railway line and the proposed Wenner-Gren railway-will fairly well parallel each other for a distance of some 200 miles.
Certainly a saving of $30 million should be acceptable to the provincial government and to the Wenner-Gren people. I understand that the route would be somewhat longer by using the Canadian National rails and right of way but that the grades are much easier, and that constructing a railway such as Wenner-Gren proposes, in fairly difficult territory, would be more costly than if they were to follow the present route of the C.N.R.
But as I said, I am of the opinion that there is more concern in Premier Bennett's mind in using this matter as an election gimmick in northern British Columbia than there is in actually building a railway and that actually, regardless of his proposed gift or sellout to the Wenner-Gren interests, this railway some time will have to come under the jurisdiction of the federal government or the federal government will have to participate in it in some way. Quite frankly, I may say I think the Canadian National Railways have missed the boat completely in not proposing or starting building that northward extension from Hazelton many years ago.
However, that is its business. Apparently the C.N.R. runs so inefficiently under Mr. Gordon that it is losing money hand over fist, and perhaps he would not think in terms of losing any more, because apparently his views are connected with the amount of mileage he has under his jurisdiction. So much for the railway which I think is a necessity, which I think should be built under a public corporation such as the Canadian National Railways, and which should have been built many years ago from Hazelton north, not by the present route from Prince George and paralleling 200 miles of C.N.R. line.
I should like to make a comment or two about coastal shipping, and perhaps I can

go into some detail on this question when the Canadian maritime commission estimates are before us. I should like to put these thoughts before the minister now, however, so that he and the officials of the maritime commission will have a full appreciation of them if they have not already such an appreciation.
We have complained of this question for a number of years. Last night I was interested to hear the hon. member for Comox-Alberni make reference to the question of coastal shipping also. While he did not go quite so far as to suggest any alternative method to that which exists now, at least he recognized the problem.
Coastal shipping in British Columbia has deteriorated tremendously in the last few years, and I would say this deterioration has increased under the Conservative government rather than lessened. I do not know whether this is the fault of the minister or whether he even knows in much detail the situation which exists with regard to coastal shipping in British Columbia. We pay an annual subsidy to Northland Navigation Company of some $294,500 a year, I think it is. That is a subvention or subsidy to provide service to isolated spots on the coast of British Columbia.
Unfortunately this Northland Navigation Company, which is in a monopoly position in many respects, is taking a rather cavalier and discriminatory attitude toward the communities it is supposed to service. I understand that Captain Terry, the owner of Northland Navigation Company, is rather friendly with the Conservative party. Perhaps this is one reason he got the contract or the subvention in the first place.
Some of the things his company does might bear relating. For instance, a year ago at Christmas time, without any warning other than some advertisements in the newspaper; without any reference to the Canadian maritime commission, something which should have been done; without any formal request being made to alter the schedule of service to these up-coast communities, Northland Navigation Company suddenly decided that they were not going to service these communities during Christmas week. This decision left many people completely isolated. It upset the Christmas mail; it upset delivery of Christmas parcels; it upset the plans of people who wanted to travel in or out of those communities at Christmas time in order to be with their families. That was done all because Northland Navigation Company is in a monopoly position and is able to do what it feels like doing, and all because it or Captain Terry is a very close friend of the party that is now in office.

I have had telegrams and letters galore from people in communities like Bella Coola, Bella Bella, Ocean Falls, and Stuart and Ellis islands over in the Queen Charlotte islands; time after time complaining about the poor, inadequate and disgraceful service that is provided to these communities by this particular company to which we pay almost $300,000 a year as a subsidy in order for them to provide that particular service. I know there was a great deal of politics involved in the decline of Union Steamships which preceded Northland Navigation Company. I do not intend to go into that matter.
Will you go into the matter of their subsidies?
The amount is $294,000.
One million dollars is what Union Steamships asked for.

Mr. Chairman, when the government considers building another bridge east of the Jacques Cartier bridge which, as everyone knows, has aroused a scandal, it should consider the possibility of building that bridge in the vicinity of St. Sulpice, in the constituency of L'Assomption.
My proposal is based on the following considerations: first, the towns of Repentigny and St. Sulpice constitute a most important housing development in the greater Montreal area; second, a bridge there would serve the highway that will soon link some of the most important centres of the province of Quebec; third, on account of Bouchard island, the cost of the bridge would be less, and would not interfere with the St. Lawrence seaway. Fourth, such a bridge would also have the advantage of linking up Montreal with the whole south shore area, which is developing into a Canadian Ruhr, over the whole section between Longueuil and Sorel. Fifth, such an outlet to the chief communities on the south shore would be a great boost to the economic development of such areas as Joliette, L'Assomption and- Montcalm, as well as the Berthier-Maskinonge area. Sixth, a bridge thus located would be a necessary counterpart to the Gardeur de Repentigny bridge, and would be a new road to progress, apart from the fact that a bridge in that area would, from a civil defence point of view, serve as a vital outlet for population centres, servicing at one and the same time four important areas, namely those of Montreal, Joliette, Sorel and Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere.
So I ask the government that if and when it considers plans for the erection of a bridge in that area, the bridge be named "Marquis de Montcalm", in memory of this national hero, or else "Frangois Labelle", one of the illustrious founders of the L'Assomption College where Sir Wilfrid Laurier was educated.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:

I wonder if this is the item under which I could ask the minister for details about marine services planned for the upper great lakes in the future so we may have some idea as to the projection of the role of the department in so far as tug service is concerned and the relationship of tug service to icebreaking service.
Mr. Chairman, we operate the icebreaker at the head of the lakes as the hon. member knows, but we do not normally charter tugs.

What I want to know is if there is an important port handling millions of tons of tonnage and there are no tugs provided by private enterprise in the area-and that is the situation that actually exists today -what leadership is the department going to take in attempting to see that there are services established there? The minister will agree that there are a number of users of tug services there, but if there is not enough consistent work there for a private enterprise institution, where does the government come into it?

Mr. Chairman, at none of the harbours under the jurisdiction of my department do we provide tug service. As I have said, we provide icebreaker services in the area, but it is up to the shipping companies to provide tug service.
I do not think the minister will deny that in the national harbours there is tug service of a kind provided by the port authorities. Is that not true?
The commercial work in the national harbours is all done by commercial tugs, which operate for the shipping interests concerned.

Let me put it this way. Will the minister have his transport officials survey the situation at the lakehead and determine whether he could lure some commercial services into supplying tug service, especially in the spring and fall. The minister knows the conundrum and the argument that the Alexander Henry, the new icebreaker, could not go into the slips. Because of her size she could cause damage to wharves and cribbing, and that kind of thing. What is the alternative? In the past it seems to have been a commercial company. If no commercial tugs are available, what are we to do about getting those slips open sooner?

In the other harbours this is all done by commercial tugs, as I have said.

With regard to the hon. member's suggestion that a conference be held with the people of the lakehead and ourselves to discuss this matter my officials tell me that they have indicated to the hon. member that we are willing to talk to him or them at any time and will welcome such talks.

One other question: Are any of the harbour commissions which have been set up developing another kind of harbour authority separate from the national harbours board? Are any of them getting into this business of providing tug services?
I will check on that, Mr. Chairman, but not to my knowledge or the knowledge of my deputy minister.

I wish to ask a question as to the scope of the Alexander Henry. It has been provided, as the minister says, for icebreaker services in the upper lakes. This does not give a great deal of flexibility in spite of the magnificent capacity of this tug to provide service all the way down to Parry Sound, Collingwood, and the area up to the lake-head, a very crucial part of the area. I wonder whether any plans are under way to give it more flexibility?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. We are studying this matter very closely. It may easily appear after those studies are over that we do need another ship, but this matter has not been decided up to the present time. It is being closely studied at the moment.
Mr. Chairman, is this the item on which I can properly ask the minister questions on how his pilotage plans on the great lakes are developing?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, any time at all.

I would be interested in hearing from the minister a statement as to how this scheme is working out and whether there is any possibility of the government getting out of this in the future and allowing those pilots to go back on a private enterprise basis? I am not asking for it; I am wondering what the government's plans are? As I understand the probable future development in relation to the United States, this whole question of pilotage in the great lakes in so far as the United States government is concerned is that they intend to keep their pilotage on a private enterprise basis.
I should like an explanation on how the two are going to dovetail when on the one hand you have a government service and on the other hand a private enterprise service?
