speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If there is no objection, I should like to say a word about the question of pilotage. I certainly was not under the impression that one was operated under government authority and the other under private enterprise authority. I was under the impression that the pilots in the various districts in Canada, while they were under the jurisdiction of the minister as the pilotage authority of Canada, none the less received their salaries under the terms of a collective agreement which was made through the shipping federation and, of course, always approved by the pilotage authority. I do not know what the position is in the United States but I am sure the minister has given consideration to the present position of the various districts in Canada. What leads me to say a word about it is that when the pilotage bill was introduced in the house last year or two years ago there was some indication in the bill that one of the districts, if not two, namely the Montreal and Quebec pilotage districts, were to be abolished. I was glad when the minister did not pursue that bill further and I hope that if a bill is introduced dealing with pilotage during this or the next session there will be no question of the Quebec and Montreal pilotage pilots disappearing, but that they will remain under the present jurisdiction.
This prompts me to ask the minister a question which I think is important. What progress has been made in the negotiations with the United States concerning pilotage on the upper St. Lawrence and great lakes? The last we heard of it was a statement made by the minister in the house in answer to questions that were asked on the orders of the day from time to time. I know that a bill was introduced in the Senate of the United States but I am not aware of its present position. However, I do not think it has gone through both houses of the United States congress. Has an agreement been negotiated with the United States? If not, is it near completion? Has it reached the point where a bill might be introduced at this session of parliament? These are matters on which the committee would wish the minister to enlighten it at this time.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. There is no written agreement with the United States on this matter, simply an understanding between

Supply-Transport
the two countries. They have just passed through both houses ol congress a bill which is very similar to ours, and similar in intent. I have a bill which I mentioned earlier this session, which I have been waiting to present to the house when I was sure that the United States legislation would go through. As a matter of fact, the bill was delivered in my hands this morning. I will be presenting it to cabinet for ratification in the next day or so. Then it will be introduced in the house. The legislation in Canada and in the United States will be very similar, indeed.
Regarding the status of pilots throughout our system, the status of pilots, other than those of the great lakes, is as described by the hon. member for Laurier. They are in various pilotage districts which he mentioned. In the great lakes they are employees of the Department of Transport by their own choice. We understand that they are very satisfied with this arrangement, and we are satisfied with it. At any time any other pilotage district wishes to enter into the same kind of arrangement we have let them know we will be very happy to have them. At the same time, we are also very pleased to have them carry on in the way they are now.
I might also add, Mr. Chairman, that this whole matter has been discussed very thoroughly with the United States. They see no problem at all arising because they have a slightly different system of pilotage than we have. They feel, and we feel, that the pilotage arrangements between the two countries will work out satisfactorily. This thing has been very thoroughly discussed between us.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I suppose until we see the bill it is not possible for us on this side, at least, to come to a conclusion in this respect. This prompts me to ask another question. In the bill which the minister intends to submit to his colleagues is there any reference to the abolishment of the pilotage districts of Montreal and Quebec?
No, emphatically no. This bill will deal only with the pilotage on the great lakes, and nothing else from last year's bill will appear in this bill.

May I ask one question here? Does the minister mean there will be nothing in the bill giving Canada authority to license foreign ships when they reach Montreal, that is license foreign ship masters to pilot on the great lakes after a certain amount of service?
The applicability of the bill is only to great lakes waters.

That still does not clear it up; foreign ships are coming into the great lakes
[Mr. Hees.)
waters and is Canada going to have the right to give the masters 'B' licences or certain licences that will enable them to operate without pilotage?
I think the hon. member will realize that he is getting a little ahead of himself because this bill still has to be passed by cabinet, and it still has to be introduced into this house.

My reason for asking the question is very clear. As the minister knows, there have been complaints from the United States pilots, who are highly organized into a union-type system. I have no particular brief for the United States pilots or the union-type system, but it seems to me they have a potential as troublemakers, let us put it, by causing dissention in all the arrangements. I gather from their complaints that they are very strongly against this particular provision. I should like to know whether there is anything in the United States legislation that is considered as protecting United States interests, as the United States unions consider it in this particular regard.
As I said a little earlier, the United States legislation provides for basically the same kind of system that we will have and which will be provided under this bill.

I should like to turn to another part of the marine service. I do not believe we have had a really fair outline from the minister-that is not necessarily his fault- as to just what his department is planning to do in connection with small boat matters in Canada. I know we have had the suggestion that there is some kind of conference, and that eventually the informal licensing arrangements that are now in existence will become formalized. Until we observe a pattern for the future in connection with this very important matter, and because of the tremendous growth in the use of small boats on Canadian waters, I should like to know also what estimate the department has of the cost in the future of administering this aspect of the work.
It seems to me that the development of small boats has become more than a hobby; it has become a summer way of life. There is going to be, I would imagine, a demand upon the treasury of this government and the provincial governments in terms of licences, facilities, policing and so on. I should like to know where we are going on this particular item. It seems to me we deserve a statement at this time.

Mr. Chairman, we believe that we are giving leadership to small boat owners all across the country in connection with

small boat safety. As the hon. member knows very well, because of the very nature of the ownership of small boats and the tremendous number of waters on which they operate, it would be difficult, if not impossible, to impose rigid regulations and police them. We have to rely, therefore, on the good sense of the small boat operators themselves to operate their boats in compliance with safety regulations which are decided to be in the best interests of the general public and the small boat operators.
Once a year there is a large conference held at which there are representatives of the provincial governments, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and all interested parties, to discuss safety measures and possible ways of bringing more and more people to realize the need for the safe handling of small boats. We believe that this is having a good effect. More and more people are becoming interested. We feel that the safety suggestions we are making are being adhered to more and more year by year.

Is it not possible for the department to make some kind of analysis of the waters where the intensity of use at the present time is such that some stiffer regulations could be applied, and some policing could be applied. I think any one of us who goes to an area such as Muskoka or anywhere on the great lakes system sees flagrant examples of dangerous conduct and very bad equipment. We have tragedies happening all the time on the water. I am just wondering if there could not be some kind of limit set where stricter licensing and policing could be put into effect. I am wondering if that is a necessary step that the department might take.

The enforcement of the regulations in connection with small boats has to be carried out, of necessity, by the provincial police and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. We have a small permanent committee of departmental officials who do nothing but work on small boat safety measures year in and year out. They are in constant communication and co-operation with the provincial police of the various provinces and with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to assist them and to set standards of small boat safety as well as to enforce those standards where that is possible. I really do not know what more we can do than we are doing. At the present time, as I say, we are working very closely with the people and with the police officers who are enforcing these regulations. We try to give them all the help we can. We try to educate small boat owners in the very best way we can.
Supply-Transport
We have a very good pamphlet called "Safety Afloat" which is sent out by the thousands and to which a great deal of attention is paid. I want to assure the hon. member and every member of the committee that this is a matter that has our constant attention. It is a most important one, and we welcome suggestions that can be made by interested groups or individuals as to what can be done to improve small boat safety.

What I was trying to suggest was that the time had arrived when more concrete steps should be taken. I think we all remember the recent tragedy of the mounted police boat on Lake Simcoe. Almost every day during the summer we have these tragedies. One notices the editorial comment and the general view is that some adequate protective measures need to be taken to protect people from themselves. I do not refer only to the standard life jackets, the standardization of boats and various safety provisions along the water thoroughfares, but to some effective way, a common way right across Canada, of getting a code for prosecution.
What I am trying to put before the minister is: has the government considered the real problem of the tremendous cost of doing a good job in this connection and the increasing demand that the job be done? I wanted to know where the department stood in connection with spending, to this particular marine service, perhaps an increasing amount of up to $10 million or $15 million in order to police the boats on the waterways and to enforce regulations and licensing requirements. I am afraid, however, that the demand for that kind of service is growing.

As I have tried to indicate, in very heavily populated areas where there is a great concentration of boating the policing is far more intense because there are more R.C.M.P. and provincial police in those areas. However, as the hon. member knows, a great deal of boating is done in lakes and rivers which are in relatively uninhabited or sparsely inhabited parts of the country where the fishing, hunting and pastimes of that sort are of the very best. To think that you could have a police force that is going to be policing every lake and river, particularly in these far out districts, is almost fantastic. However, I want to assure the hon. member that we receive the utmost of co-operation from all of the small boat manufacturers.
A step that has been accomplished in the last few months is that they now put on every boat a metal plate which specifies the maximum power that should be applied to that particular hull and the maximum load

Supply-Transport
that boat should carry. As I think the hon. member will realize, it that practice had been adhered to in the sad case to which he has just referred I think that accident would not have happened. We are learning as we go along. As a result of these conferences we are being able to move forward, I think steadily, in this regard.
Another thing we do is to encourage the inspection at all times of the life-saving equipment which boats carry. As a matter of fact, a friend of mine protested most vigorously to me last year because the R.C.M.P. had caused him some trouble by telling him that the life-saving equipment he had was not satisfactory and by confiscating it because they felt it was dangerous for him to have it in his boat. However, things of that kind are going on all the time.
I hope I have answered the hon. member's question. We are doing more and more in this regard. It is a very big field. Because of the fact that the people who use small boats are running on literally many thousands of bodies of waters all across the country, the actual policing is a difficult thing; but the provincial police and the R.C.M.P. co-operate to the very utmost of of their ability.

May I ask the minister whether he could just indicate where in the estimates we can get some kind of estimate of the people who are working in this particular field across the country so that we can get some idea of the scope of the present service and the amount of money that is spent on it?

Our service is supervisory and it is here in Ottawa. As I say, there is a small committee that is working all the time to provide information for those who need and can best use that information. The people who do the policing are the provincial police and the R.C.M.P. Our department does not have a police force to enforce these regulations. We are available at all times to give advice. We send out this pamphlet "Safety Afloat". We conduct meetings once a year of all interested parties. We are prepared to give advice, assistance and help at any time; but we cannot operate a force across this country in order to try to give instruction in and enforce the regulations. As I say, we work with the R.C.M.P. and with the provincial police. They are extremely co-operative. We give them all the advice and help that we can give them. We do the same thing for the boat manufacturers who are extremely co-operative. We work closely with boat users and anybody who is interested. However, we have not employees all across the country engaged in enforcing the small boat regulations.
Can the minister give an estimate of the number of people involved in this work and what the fixed cost would be for a year?

Outside of the publication of the pamphlet I am advised that the fixed costs would be somewhere between $30,000 and $40,000; but a lot of work that is carried on in this regard is done by a great many people on a voluntary basis, as in so many other volunteer organizations across the country who are interested in safety work and so on.

I should like to ask a few more questions on this matter. As to this attempt at voluntary licensing that has been established, may I ask where the records are kept? I am referring to voluntary licensing. I understand there has been voluntary licensing of small craft. I should like to know where the records are kept and who is going to be responsible for these records as they increase and to keep them up to date.
The registration is compulsory for boats only. The registration is kept by the Department of National Revenue because the customs officers do the registering of these boats.

I was wondering whether the minister could tell us if there has been any consultation with the United States in connection with life-saving on the great lakes. I recollect that two or three years ago a resolution concerning a coastguard service on the great lakes was debated. I also understand that it is a live subject in the minds of many people who have been close to catastrophe over the last two or three years. I am wondering whether there is any coordinated arrangement between the provinces and the federal government with regard to, for example, air search. Are local fishermen alerted to be on hand if something like this happens? What I have in mind is this. Last summer a boat was out on Georgian bay for between 30 hours and 40 hours and it was not found. By good luck the wind turned and blew it in to shore. I am just wondering whether any work is being done in the department or whether any move is being made in the department to co-ordinate something along the life-saving line.

We studied this matter very intensely and we came to the conclusion that what are needed mainly are co-ordinators who will first of all direct the boats in any particular area that could be used for going to the rescue of a ship or boat in distress. We have appointed a co-ordinator for the east coast and for the west coast. I am advised that the board is sitting today to choose a

co-ordinator for the great lakes. His job will be to assist and to work with the shipping or boating interests in the great lakes so that a method can be worked out whereby, when a disaster occurs, the available craft in that area would go to the assistance of the ship or boat in distress.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I know that everybody connected with the small boat industry has been greatly interested in the matter of life jackets and safety equipment that has been worn for a number of years or has been obtained in the last year or so but is of no value and/ or sometimes even dangerous. I understood that the department was doing some work on examining all types of life-saving equipment or life-preserving equipment and that it was expected that before too long there would be range of equipment put out as to which the department themselves would assume responsibility as having approved it. I am wondering whether that work has been finalized.

Yes; that has been done. The department approves certain types of lifesaving equipment. The Department of Transport's stamp is put on such equipment so that it can readily be seen by police who might inspect life-saving equipment in a craft. The law requires that life-saving equipment in a craft have the stamp of the Department of Transport on it or it is not considered satisfactory and cannot be passed as satisfactory equipment for life-saving.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Might I ask if the manufacturer puts this on after approval has been given or do inspectors go round authorizing its use? If so, is it done with numbers so that one manufacturer uses one number so you can check back and see when equipment coming on the market does not meet the specifications and see who is responsible for its manufacture?
Our steamship inspection staff do the actual stamping and approving of the equipment after it has been actually tested.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am not sure whether this matter comes under the marine section but I am sure the minister will have no objections if I raise it. We have a number of problems connected with the upkeep of navigation on lake Timiskaming for boating purposes. One of the major problems in relation to the small boats is the number of logs and other material floating around. Provincially, in some lakes like lake Timagami, they have reached an agreement of some description where the sweeping has to be done before June 13. After that the party leaving logs in the water in that area is responsible for any
Supply-Transport
damage done. Previous to June 15 the companies are assumed to have jurisdiction over the waterway and if you drive a boat in the lake that is your responsibility. But after June 15 I think the companies are responsible, and if you sink your boat or get a hole in it, as I say they are responsible.
In lake Timiskaming we have a different problem which has been with us for 75 years I suppose, because the Upper Ottawa Improvement Company which was set up under federal charter many years ago assumed the responsibility for all the driving and handling of logs on the tributaries of the Ottawa and on lake Timiskaming. They have had many problems which are really not of their own making. The effect of the floods was bad this year and has created a problem not quite in keeping with a normal year. They are a small company now but there are still a great number of logs coming into lake Timiskaming continually throughout the year. I understand from talking to people in the Ottawa section that over the whole length of the Ottawa river there is the same problem.
When we have objected to the Department of Transport and asked that these lakes be cleaned up, they say they are not responsible for this. When you talk to the Upper Ottawa Improvement Company they say that they are doing it as fast as they can but that they have limited resources. As far as I know they have accepted no responsibility to a third party.
In lake Timiskaming, particularly in the Haileybury and New Liskeard areas, although they are on a bay of the lake, there are hundreds of small craft. At the present time the lake is literally dotted with deadheads and stuff as high as a quarter of a mile up the shore because of the flood this year. This has all drifted out into the lake and is a terrific hazard to navigation. In fact it makes it almost impassable.
I think something can be done about this. The department itself could take some action with regard to this stuff coming in. As far as Wabi bay is concerned, which is the main boating section at New Liskeard and Haileybury, I think that while it is an expensive proposition control booms across the bay would be a lot less expensive than the damage caused at the moment. This is something that I think could be enforced and I think the department should exercise more control over this problem than they do at present. It is a real hazard and the problem will become so bad that as far as I can see thousands of pulp logs and pieces of saw timber will be cruising around on the lake all summer. The company now sweeping it

Supply-Transport
has only several small steamers and a limited number of people to work on them.
I think regulations should be enforced prohibiting a company from allowing these logs to go out. In normal circumstances a company will double move and put in a control boom half a mile down the river. It may have three or four controls on it. But none of these companies exercise that type of control and have no objection at all if the logs go down to the lake.
I sympathize with the Upper Ottawa Improvement Company this year because flood conditions have been unusual and have created a problem which is not normal; but in normal years it is very seldom that these logs are cleaned up until late September when the boating season is over.
I would like to know if the minister has any suggestion to make to help solve the problem. It may be that as far as the department is concerned their interest is in giving lakes like lake Timiskaming and those on the Ottawa river back to the provincial government, although if they are interprovincial difficulty arises as to the border line between two provinces. In Ontario where the provincial government looks after the lakes they are much better looked after than where the federal government is in authority, because in my experience it continually keeps passing the buck to other people involved.

The situation which the hon. member has just described is a very real and worrying one. Unfortunately logging comes under provincial jurisdiction. As there is quite naturally a conflict of jurisdiction in this matter it complicates the enforcement of regulations prohibiting the kind of behaviour which the hon. member has suggested. What we try to do is to work with the logging companies and to point out to them the dangers which their logs are causing and I think we have been reasonably successful in most cases. We have found, however, that really the most effective deterrent to allowing their logs to get out of control and become troublesome to small boats is the pressure which can be brought to bear by the local residents on the logging company itself.
However, it is a real problem and one about which we try to do everything we can to bring about satisfactory results. As I say the main difficulty is that the jurisdiction is a divided one and it complicates the question to a great extent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
In this case it is not a divided jurisdiction because the Upper Ottawa Improvement Company is a federal company which was set up with full jurisdiction over the upper Ottawa river, lake Timiskaming,

the Ottawa river and so on. No company, as I understand from reading the act which set up the Upper Ottawa Improvement Company, has any right to drive logs on lake Timiskaming, up on the Ottawa river or in any area around there. They have to pay the Upper Ottawa Improvement Company so much money for using their lakes.
As far as the provincial question is concerned, the logs which bother us in lake Timiskaming on the Ontario side do not come from Ontario at all; they are Quebec logs which come down the riviere des Quinze and other rivers in that area. But no logs are driven on the Ottawa river; for years no logs have been driven down there.
This is the situation which I think the government could do something about, because they are under charter through the federal government here. It is a very simple act. The act, which was written back in Queen Victoria's time, said that if they do not operate in the interests of the community and the people, the act will be forfeited. Certainly over the years they have not acted too much in the interests of the people. The minister says what is needed is some reaction from the communities concerned. I can assure him that this reaction comes to me, unfortunately, first of all. Then if I do not get anything done about it they go to the minister and others. But I usually hear about it as early as anybody.
The people sympathize with them in the problem they have in a year like this, but it was just as bad last year and the year before. It was even as bad when there was very little water in the lake. I should like to know what can be done to solve it on a permanent basis. It has been suggested that the communities in my area should get together, that a dozen men in motorboats should sweep the logs on their own and charge the companies for booming. If something does not happen, somebody is going to burn these logs which are piled up all along the shore. I happen to have a property there and one of my neighbours has 30 cords of wood piled up ready to burn. I do not think that is the right way of handling the problem.
I shall be glad to look into the situation to which the hon. member has drawn my attention.

I wanted to turn to something which has to do with pilotage and I now have the papers involved. The minister will remember that earlier this session I asked a question in relation to the shipping federation of Canada. The question was No. 73 and it read:
Has the department ever given the shipping federation any authority or aproval for it to present

the views of the government of Canada on pilotage to any United States congressional committee?
I should like to read from a committee report. It is the report of a hearing before the subcommittee on coastguard, coast and geodetic survey and navigation of the committee on merchant marine and fisheries of the house of representatives, eighty sixth congress, first session, on Bill H.R. 57 to require pilots on certain vessels navigating United States waters of the great lakes, and for other purposes. During the cross-examination of Mr. Brisset, who was a spokesman for the shipping federation of Canada, Mr. Dorn, a member of the committee said:
Does the speaker speak for the Canadian government?
To which the reply was:
I think I will say "Yes".
The report continues:
In other words, the Canadian government is threatening the United States to close off those waters unless the United States refuses to pass this bill? I cannot believe that, sir.
Perhaps I have gone too far.
I think perhaps you have, sir.
I will not say that I am speaking for the Canadian government here. I am trying to explain-
But you are implying that you do speak for the Canadian government, however.

I think I can explain that without there being any need for the hon. member to read further. This case is, of course, very well known to me. The shipping federation had no authority whatever to speak for the Canadian government. They did so on their own, and as soon as we found out what the federation had said and done we reprimanded them severely for so doing. We also informed the United States government that they were not speaking for the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How did you reprimand them, by slapping their backs?
As I remember it, we spoke to them rather sharply.

The minister, in his reply to my question, said the matter was taken up on May 29, 1959 at a meeting of officials with the pilotage committee of the shipping federation.
This raises a matter which is bothering me as one who is, in a sense, an involuntary spokesman for some of the pilots. Since many of the pilots have now become civil servants it has been suggested that the shipping federation has become a spokesman for some of the policies followed by the government. There have been complaints that the shipping federation has had the ear of the Department of Transport right down the line. Whatever the Department of Transport does usually
Supply-Transport
follows the policies of the shipping federation of Canada. This being the argument, I want to ask the minister if he has received from the St. Lawrence river pilots a review of the situation by the shipping federation of Canada and, if he has, I should like to know if he is in agreement with the following suggestion made by the federation on page 8 of the pamphlet. These read as follows:
It is the opinion and recommendation of the Shipping Federation of Canada, Inc., that a system of dealing with the pilotage situation should be evolved which would:
1)	Pay the pilots fairly and adequately in relation to their competence and the service performed.
2)	Remove, permanently, as a subject of discussion with pilots, the tariffs which are to be applied to the shipping industry. It is the opinion of the federation that this can and should be done by establishing a non-political commission to administer pilotage and to determine-after discussion with pilots and shipping interests-fair levels of remuneration for them. Matters of tariffs, service charges and other assessments against the industry would be worked out between the commission and representatives of the shipping industry.
The present monopolistic position of the pilots is capable of creating serious discrepancies between services performed and the cost of the service. Instability of pilotage service can affect not only the shipping industry but the entire Canadian economy adversely. The present system is conducive to instability, and is deteriorating rapidly. The Shipping Federation of Canada Inc. regards it as most urgent to establish immediately a system of pilotage which will ensure-
Eight points are then listed, and I do not wish to take up time by reading them all. What I should like to ask is this: are these, now, the objectives of his department and, if not, what are his department's views?

To go back to the first question which was asked. The hon. member says that the shipping federation has the ear of the department. I can assure him that the shipping federation quite often says to us that the pilots have the ear of the government. We get it from both sides. We have meetings with both parties quite often and we listen with great interest to what each side has to say. Then we try to work out the best possible policy from the point of view of the pilots and the shippers.
With regard to the pamphlet which the hon. member has mentioned, I am aware of the pamphlet but I do not want to comment on the question which was raised. I may say that no federation makes government policy.

Could the minister tell me whether the dominion marine association or the lake carriers association have recently presented their views on the pilotage situation to the minister and, if so, what are those views?

It depends on what the hon. member means by "recently". They meet with us two or three times a year. We would have

Supply-Transport
to know the subject to which the hon. member is referring, or the time. Whenever we get together, pilotage is always one of the subjects that come up for discussion.

What I meant by "recently" is that there have been indications from the annual meetings-they usually have a joint meeting with the lake carriers-.that their objections were much more in line with those of the United States pilots' union than with the views of the shipping federation of Canada. Anyway, there is a conflict of views here, and I should like to know something about how this is to be resolved, and what is the attitude of the department.

I should like to assure the hon. member that the government is not dictated to in these matters by the shipping federation or the dominion marine association or by the pilots group. We meet with them all. We listen to them all and we try to adopt the best policy we can. Nobody is telling us what to do in their own particular interest.

I should like to read an extract which appeared at page 43 of the October 1, 1959 issue of Fairplay magazine:
In a recent article which appeared in an American magazine, Mr. Carl E. McDowell, executive vice president of the American institute of marine underwriters, referred to some of the problems which were confronting underwriters with regard to the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. He said that the records of the American institute of marine underwriters had reported 62 casualties or accidents to vessels in the St. Lawrence river, the seaway, and the lakes since the seaway opened (to June 19) compared with 39 in the same period in 1958. (This is exclusive of fishing vessels and barges, and ice damage.) Many of these accidents, however, were of a kind which marine underwriters have come to associate with this new approach which makes an "eighth sea" of the great lakes. Many of the vessels now entering the lakes have never done so before. Their masters and crews, no matter how able and experienced in ocean navigation have little or no experience with the especially difficult narrow and restricted passages which constitute much of the seaway. "Rules of the road" for navigation in the seaway and great lakes differ in many respects from those used on the high seas. Mr. McDowell said marine underwriters were hopeful that legislation would be passed by both Canada and the United States which would require experienced great lakes pilots to be aboard all vessels using the seaway and the lakes. They supported a bill sponsored by the United States coast guard which would have accomplished a good part of this aim. Unfortunately, however, this legislation was not passed during the last session of congress and is still pending.
The viewpoint expressed therein is that there has been an increasing number of accidents on the lakes as a result of foreign shipping coming in and that they stem from the unfamiliarity of the foreign masters with the rules of the road and all the difficulties of narrow and restricted passages. Would the
[Mr. Hees.l
minister inform us what the record indicates in the first year of the seaway operations and this year as far as the accident pattern is concerned and if there has been the marked shift that this article alleges has occurred?
I do not have that specific information available at the moment but I shall be glad to secure it for the hon. member and give it to him.

The minister will admit that this type of allegation lends some support to the stand of the admiral of the United States coastguard and of those people who argue that foreign shipping should have Canadian or United States pilots on board. I would appreciate the minister giving us a summary of the experience in this regard. Is there an increased danger of accidents as a result of foreign ships being within the great lakes waterways? If so, what is the incidence of accidents and what steps could be taken to solve the problem if it exists?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed to follow up what the hon. member for Port Arthur has said. I think there is no doubt but that because of the additional number of ships and particularly foreign vessels that have come into the waterway there has been an increased number of accidents but that was to be expected. I am sure that when you have mariners who are not familiar with the canals and who have never operated an ocean-going ship in inland waters, particularly having regard to the winds and other elements, on the canals and the great lakes, there would be an increased number of accidents. I feel sure, however, that with the experience of 1959 behind us there will be in 1960 fewer accidents than in the previous year because the masters and mates will be more familar with the route and also because of the precautions that I am sure will be taken by both entities, the St. Lawrence seaway authority and the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation.
I had the opportunity of speaking with one of the members of the St. Lawrence seaway corporation at Massena not long ago. He gave it as his opinion that while it was true there had been a number of accidents caused by inexperience and curiosity seekers from overseas on the great lakes he was sure that in 1960 these accidents would be substantially reduced.

I think the hon. member for Laurier has put the case very well. As I say, I shall be glad to get these figures for the hon. member for Port Arthur. I will certainly have them by the time the bill dealing with pilotage comes before us and perhaps even

before that. As soon as I have them I will let the hon. member for Port Arthur have them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What is the liability of foreign ships that use and damage the canal system without pilotage, particularly if damage is caused to property owned by the authority as a result of the inability of the ship's officers to understand the rules?

It depends on the nature of the accident. If it is a slight accident and one which it is considered has come about through no fault of the master there probably would be no recourse taken but if it is a serious accident of any kind with a considerable amount of damage these cases may all be taken up in the courts between the government and the shipping company concerned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let me give an example. At Cornwall last year a boat took out one gate. I was there shortly afterwards and was told it happened regularly. The masters on the ships did not understand the signals used and were not used to judging distances in cramped quarters.

It would all depend on our assessment of the case as to whether or not we considered the master of the ship had been negligent. If we considered the accident had occurred through no fault of the master because of conditions beyond his control or some mistake on our part or on the part of the canal authority in not signalling him properly we would not proceed against the company. If we considered that the damage was caused by negligence on the part of the ship, however, then we would certainly prosecute.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What would happen if one of our licensed pilots had been hired to pilot the ship? Where does the difference lie?
It would not make any difference at all, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If one of our pilots was hired to bring the ship in and an accident occurred due to negligence would the company be prosecuted for the negligence of our pilot?
The master is always in charge of the ship. The pilot is only an adviser.

Hon. members will remember the Baffin incident and the crash at Black Rock when there was some question as to whether the master was in charge of the vessel.
Has the Canadian merchant seamen's service guild made protests to the department as a consequence of the aide memoire tabled in this house and appearing in Hansard of
Supply-Transport
February 23, 1960? I ask that question because I received a number of letters from members of the guild advising me that they were taking up this matter with the government very strongly. Their argument is that the Canadian government should not issue pilot licenses class B to masters and officers of foreign ships giving them the right to pilot their own ships through the great lakes open waters with certain conditions of examination. This is one of the pressure groups the minister referred to and I want to know the scope of the pressure and what reply was sent.
I have not that information. I will certainly look it up and see if we did, and if we did I will advise the hon. member.

I have a few more questions. I should like the minister to explain what is the future of the pilotage situation at Kingston? At the present time there are four employees at Kingston, and they are employed as dispatchers under the Civil Service Act. I want to know whether this is going to continue and whether they are still going to have pilots dispatched out of Kingston, or is the whole service there likely to die as the port of Kingston does less and less business?

No, Mr. Chairman. We provide dispatchers who are civil servants in all the pilotage districts and there is nothing peculiar about Kingston; it is no different from any other district. We do not have any plans to make any change.

I know from discussions that there are people in Kingston who are worried about the future of Kingston as a port and whether there will be any pilotage offered there in the future because of the nature of the traffic which is by-passing Kingston. I wanted some kind of assurance that this service was going to be kept on.
Yes, Mr. Chairman. The service will continue to be available at Kingston.

I wanted to get more of an explanation from the minister than the one he gave in answer to some questions on the order paper. Part 5 of question 72 was as follows:
What fees did the government collect from its pilotage service in the great lakes?
This was in 1959: and the answer was:
$348,428, plus an indeterminable amount for travelling expenses of headquarters officers and administration costs absorbed in the headquarters vote.
Part 6 of the question was:
What was the difference between the income and expense of this service?

Supp ly-Transport
The answer was:

In other words, ostensibly we have a profit of about $120,000 on the arrangement, but we have this indeterminable amount. Can the minister give us some kind of an estimate of this indeterminable amount? I know the minister is not sympathetic to extension of government service-heaven forbid. That is against his line but here he has extended the government service. I know he would want to make absolutely sure that the government is not going into the hole if it can redeem its charges for the service and show a profit. I should like to have a clearer picture of this indeterminable amount. I should like to be absolutely sure that the department plans to continue to make a profit in this particular service.

I am advised that it will be very difficult to segregate that particular item. The profit would be considerably greater than the administration expenses, but I am afraid I cannot break it down exactly.
Does the minister think there is still a substantial margin of profit?
Yes, there is still a substantial profit but it has been partly taken up by salary increases for the pilots.

That is the next question I wanted to ask. I have received complaints from several of the pilots that they were not fully paid last year on their contracts. Their contracts died when they got their new schedule. I wanted to know what substance there was in that, that they were hired for a certain period and were not paid for the full period last year?
I am advised that all of the pilots were fully paid from the day they came on but not necessarily from the beginning of the pilotage season; but they were all fully paid from the time they came on.

Item agreed to.
409. Construction or acquisition of vessels and equipment, $6,500,000.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to call the minister's attention to the need for faster and improved service on the C.N.R. line between St. John's and Argentia. Argen-tia is the western terminal for the C.N.R. coastal boats which run from that port to Port aux Basques. The distance is only 80 miles but the trip takes about six or seven hours. There are no eating facilities on the train; there are no means of getting a meal along the route, and when one gets to Argentia around two or three or four in the afternoon there are no facilities at Argentia except

on board the boat. This situation could be improved first by putting on a rail liner for passengers only because the present passenger car is hitched on to a freight train. If this is not feasible, then I think it would be better if the C.N.R. were asked to employ a bus for passengers on this service. I would be grateful if the minister would bring this to the attention of the C.N.R. authorities.
I shall be glad to, Mr. Chairman.

Can the minister indicate what the general position or policy is on the matter of allocating or letting contracts to the various shipyards in Canada? I know this will be a reiteration but I should like to have it on the record so that I can use it in my local situation.
There has been some rather sharp disappointment that no contracts have gone to our particular shipyards lately. I should like some indication as to why this has happened. I am sure there are reasons and I should like the minister's explanation.

We allocate only emergency repairs where we have no choice and have no time to call tenders. Regarding certain areas, if a ship is in a certain area and has to be repaired and there is time to call tenders, then we would call tenders within the particular area. All new ship construction is by tender, not allocation.

Did the minister see a complaint from the head, I believe the retiring president, of the shipbuilders association, about the parlous condition in which shipyards are at the present time? I know we can talk about this matter when we are dealing with the estimates of the Canadian maritime commission. I gather from the remarks of this gentleman, as quoted in the newspapers, that there is some discouragement over the fact that there has been such a marked decrease this year in the estimate compared with last year. I should like the minister to explain this more fully than he did in his introductory statement, as to why there was this very sharp cut. Is it a fact that the department is pretty well up to its maximum in the kind of equipment it wants? Does it need very little more equipment?

The reason there is a decrease is that we have passed the peak of our ship construction program at the present time. I am told that other departments are building more than in past years, but so far as our department is concerned we built a number of ships in the last two or three years and you cannot keep on building at a peak of that kind forever.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I ask a question in connection with the district of Montreal and Quebec. Is it the intention to add to the icebreaker fleet that is now in operation in Montreal? If I understand properly there are three icebreakers, the McLean, the Lapointe and I think the d'Iberville, which break the ice consistently from Three Rivers upriver to Montreal. Is it the intention to change the operation of those three ships?
The next question is, is it the intention to add to the icebreaker fleet in the district of Quebec so that there will be no doubt about winter navigation in so far as the port of Quebec is concerned?

First of all, we intend to maintain a fleet of three icebreakers in the district to which the hon. member has referred between Montreal and Quebec to do the icebreaking chore which has been done for many years.
With regard to his second question, I may say we have no new icebreakers in our program for this year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is it the intention of the department or of the government to encourage winter navigation up to the port of Quebec?

Perhaps this would answer the hon. member's question. The department has supported with icebreakers the important developments on the north shore of Quebec. This traffic, which has been in resources of the hinterland, would for the most part proceed directly overseas, and into the maritimes and benefit, and I believe has benefited substantially during the past winter the suppliers in this area. The department has also supported the coastal traffic from Quebec city to the same area and for the same reason. It is not the policy of the government to take action to assist one part of the country to the detriment of another. The policy of the department in this case avoids this, while at the same time supporting new developments on the north shore which are a straight addition to the strength of the economy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I gather from this that it is the intention to support winter navigation to the north shore settlements, but a similar policy will not necessarily be followed in so far as the city of Quebec is concerned.

We believe that the requirements of the north shore are completely different from the requirements of the south shore. I have explained the particular situation on the north shore that requires winter navigation. It is the fact that there are no railways on the north shore to supply these particular ports such as Baie Comeau, Seven Islands and so on, during the winter. It is considered, therefore, most essential for the
Supply-Transport
development of that particular part of the country that navigation be kept open during the winter. The same situation does not obtain on the south shore.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister is making a distinction between the north and south shores. I am talking about Quebec which is on the north bank of the St. Lawrence river. I wonder if the policy which the minister has advocated for the north shore of the province of Quebec and along the gulf of St. Lawrence also applies to the north shore of the St. Lawrence river up to the city of Quebec?

I do not think I can make it any more clear than I have. I have outlined our policy in regard to keeping navigation open during the winter to serve the ports on the north shore to which there is no railway service. I think the hon. member will realize, if he looks at the figures, that the port of Quebec did very well this winter. It showed quite a marked increase in shipments into and out of that port during the wintertime. I feel that the policy which the government adopted during this past year in this regard worked out satisfactorily for all concerned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank the minister for that statement. I think the record will speak for itself. Can I pursue the matter upriver? Has the department been giving any consideration to a means, other than icebreaking equipment, to keep the channel open from Three Rivers to Montreal? At one time-I think I asked this question last year-some consideration was being given or at least some study was being given to the bubbler process. Have the departmental officials studied the bubbler process, and is it being given any consideration for the St. Lawrence river or any other part of Canada coming under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport?
The national research council has looked into this method and it has been found to be satisfactory for harbour use and wharf use, but not for channel use. It is impractical for channel use.

I should like to ask the minister a question. The chairman of the committee is not in a position to speak for himself, but I should like to know if the minister has a spare icebreaker he could send to the port of Toronto. They need an icebreaker up there along with the rest of the ports.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order.

Supply-Transport
I should like to ask the minister if consideration is being given to providing the services of an icebreaker for the port of Churchill during the latter part of the shipping season this fall.
I am advised that during this past winter we operated an icebreaker in that area as long as there was any need for it, and we will do the same thing next year.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw to the minister's attention, in connection with the acquisition of engines for Department of Transport vessels, the fact that there are really no diesel manufacturers in Canada. There are two firms that manufacture under United States licence. They import a great number of parts. When the department is analysing bids it should be remembered that the main turboelectric drive includes electrical equipment which is made in Canada as well as the diesel engines. The component which is of imported manufacture is the main diesel engine, and although there is a preference given to Canadian suppliers, there is a limited amount of Canadian labour content in these engines and the auxiliaries as well.
We in the west are very conscious of the fact that we want to promote increased trade with the United Kingdom which happens to be the principal manufacturer in the world of diesel engines. There are European countries whose engines are offered for sale in this country. I want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that in those cases such bids should be looked at very carefully to ensure that there is a proper assessment of the real Canadian content in the equipment being offered, and not just a make-believe, fake amount of Canadian content, and that in making these decisions proper recognition should be given to the effect such decisions would have on our export trade.
I am in a bit of a dilemma, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is surprising.

It might surprise the hon. member but it would not surprise many others. As I say, Mr. Chairman, I am in a bit of a dilemma as to when I can raise this particular subject. It has to do with the Navigable Waters Protection Act. It arises because of the offshore drilling that has been going on in some of the great lakes. I was told that it was actually a matter for the Department of Public Works. The act is actually in three or four parts and the only part that affects public works is that dealing with the issue of these temporary permits or
[The Deputy Chairman.]
permanent permits to construct a platform upon which to erect a drilling rig. Everything else affects the Department of Transport. If I am out of order, Mr. Chairman, you will appreciate the fact that I will be brief but we will probably know where I can raise this matter.
My contention is that the minor part of the act is simply the permit to construct a platform upon which to erect a drilling rig. The reason I am raising this matter here on the estimates of the Department of Transport is this. As every hon. member knows, down in Michigan, which is not too far from where I happen to live, there was a gusher last fall. I referred to it a few weeks ago, but because of the seriousness of what might happen, I think it needs repetition.
In that particular case some 50,000 barrels of oil were spilled out and for some three or four days, according to our authority, it would have covered all of lake Huron, lake St. Clair and lake Erie. The point I am trying to make is this. I should like to have the minister and his departmental officials discuss the matter on a very high level because an ignited cigarette or a match thrown overboard could have meant terrific loss of life together with an enormous amount of damage. As everyone knows, as you look across from lake Huron on the bridge you can always see 20 ships, 30 ships or 40 ships. This is a serious matter. If I am out of order, that is all right but I am glad that I brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Transport.

I should like to say a few words on a related type of matter. The minister will recall that last year I raised the question of the tragedy in which four people were killed when one of these drilling rigs collapsed. I just wondered whether, as a result of that tragedy, the minister's department or officials were keeping any closer check upon radio licensing. The whole situation comes under a host of different authorities. I think the Ontario fuel board has something to do with it. I think the Department of Transport has something to do with it. I should like to know whether any steps are taken to tighten up the checks on these drilling rigs in order to make sure that those that are some distance off shore have adequate radio facilities. As I understand the situation, this particular tragedy would probably not have happened if there had been adequate radio communication or radio communication that was up to date. I should like to have a report on that particular matter.
We do not have the authority to require a drilling rig to use a radio. However, if they use one, we inspect it, license it and make sure that it meets specifications.

I wanted to ask something in connection with the construction of icebreakers. Any of us who looked at the recent report on ice conditions in the gulf of St. Lawrence that recently became available to us I think will have come to some conclusions. I realize that this is just the beginning of a pattern of study but we have had previous studies in connection with the water route into the Churchill area. All of these indicate that with modern technology, especially in terms of the size of icebreakers- and we can take all kinds of lessons from Russia here-we can extend our shipping season in a number of places in this country to a remarkable degree. The minister has made a statement that apparently satisfied the hon. member for Laurier with regard to the position of this government vis-a-vis more winter shipping up to Quebec and up to Montreal.
I cannot be quite that satisfied and I am not speaking from a political point of view. I should like to know what is in the minister's mind when he says that this government is not going to encourage the development of services in one part of this country to the detriment of another. I think this matter has been well expressed by the Toronto Globe and Mail. I cannot give the minister the reference to this particular paper but I recall that they took up this issue. Their argument was that if it was cheaper, despite the expenditures on icebreakers, to bring ocean shipping up to Quebec and even to Montreal for a full 12-month season rather than bringing it from Halifax and Saint John, this should be gone ahead with. I am not subscribing to the Globe and Mail point of view but I think it raises the issue of the minister providing us with more than just a statement that he is not going to do something here to the detriment of something else.
There may be such great advantages to Montreal and Quebec having winter shipping that we should seriously consider it. When we get a situation such as the one the minister mentioned yesterday at Sioux Lookout, the people in Sioux Lookout are told when their railway facilities are mdved out and their employees are moved: you have just caught up with automation; you cannot stand in the way of the railway providing cheaper and more efficient service. I am not suggesting that we have reached that stage at Halifax and Saint John. However, I should like to know whether the minister is examining the situation from an economic point of view. What lies behind his statement that he is not going to encourage the development of a service that is going to be a detriment to another part of the country? What I should like to know is this. Can he guarantee us that it will be cheaper in the long run for
Supply-Transport
shippers to continue to have their winter supplies come through Halifax and Saint John than to have them come up to Quebec and Montreal?

As I said on an earlier occasion, one of the principles on which this government was elected and one of the principles that we follow is that we were elected to serve all ten provinces or the people in all ten provinces, not one or two or three or any other number. We also feel that the people in all those ten provinces have a right to a livelihood, the right to work, the right to earn a living, the right to bring up their families. It is a well-known fact that the two ports of Saint John and Halifax rely to a large extent on the shipping which goes into those ports during the five winter months when shipping on the St. Lawrence does not operate. If we do what the hon. member has urged us to do-that is if all shipping came up the St. Lawrence, if it would be cheaper to do so and all shipping went to St. Lawrence ports-then the shipping that would normally go into Halifax and Saint John simply would not go there and the people who relied on working in the harbour-the stevedores, port employees and so on-simply would be out of a job. The hon. member and his party have always appeared to be sympathetic to those who are put out of work and it surprises me when the suggestion is made that in order to provide cheaper shipping to the rest of Canada we should simply close down the ports of Halifax and Saint John and do all our shipping up through the St. Lawrence river.
I am afraid I cannot agree with that point of view. I have a great respect and liking for the people of the maritimes, the people of Halifax and Saint John. They are fine people and have a right to live and a right to a job. I do not intend to be part of spending federal funds to deprive those people of the right to work. I hope I have made myself clear to the hon. member.

That is the very point I wanted the minister to come to. I was not advocating one thing or the other, but we have the argument that the minister represents the party who was going to bring business-like efficiency into government. I was going to suggest to him, as our party has in the past, that there are other standards than dollars and cents. But what is the difference, except in scale and political power, between what is happening in a small railway community and what is potentially the situation-

speechtext:
Order. I think the Chair has been very lenient on this matter but I do not think under this item we should be discussing the economic status of one port

Supply-Transport
compared with another. I suggest the hon. member comes back to the item.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I agree the Chair has been lenient.
Coming back to the construction or acquisition of vessels and equipment, perhaps the minister can be sharply definitive. He is not going to provide any further extensions of service in terms of icebreakers for the St. Lawrence river up to the port of Montreal other than exist at the present time? Is that correct?
Mr. Speaker, I have told the committee my general philosophy on this subject which is the philosophy of this government. I do not think I can make it any clearer.

One last question on this item concerning the construction and acquisition of vessels and equipment. We have all been taken with the magnificent accomplishment of the Russians in producing an atomic powered icebreaker. I gather it has been the decision of this government not to go into that particular field. As a result of the operating experience which the Russians have had, which I understand has been most favourable, I wonder whether any reconsideration is being given to this matter? Whatever the case I would like to know what is the cost factor so far as an atomic powered icebreaker is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, we are very much interested in the possibilities of atomic icebreakers. We are carrying on a very intensive study of this whole matter in a British shipyard at the present time where such matters are being studied very thoroughly.
At the present time, to build an atomic icebreaker the same size and power as, for instance, our biggest icebreaker would cost twice as much and three times as much to operate. We just feel that the economics do not justify our going into the atomic icebreaker field at the present time. However, this matter is being very thoroughly examined all the time and we are keeping abreast of the situation. I am advised that the particular research product in which we are sharing will be completed by next spring and that we will have a report on it at that time.

Has the minister or his officials any indication how well the Russian icebreaker is working out? I have seen phenomenal stories about what it can do and despite the cost differential, if it can do what the Russians claim for it it promises to be a sensational vessel for our Arctic region.
[The Deputy Chairman.]

Our information is that the Russian atomic icebreaker is working very well but an atomic icebreaker does not work any better than a conventional icebreaker, such as the ones we use. The advantage of an atomic icebreaker is that it can stay away from its home base much longer than a conventional type of icebreaker. This is of course more important to the Russians because the particular type of job they do requires ships which can stay away a long period of time. We are not faced with the same problem as they to anywhere near the same extent. It is largely a matter of balancing economics against what an icebreaker is required to do.

Mr. Chairman, while the minister is in this mood of magnanimity which he has just expressed toward the people of the maritimes I wonder if he could tell the committee what the government is doing or would be prepared to do with regard to the establishment of a transshipment port at Mortier bay?
We certainly do not have any plans for such a port at the present time. It is an interesting idea and this government, being progressive, is always interested in interesting ideas.
Is there anything concrete the minister can report to the house at the moment?
No, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, could the minister tell the committee whether any negotiations have taken place with the government of Newfoundland with a view to having St. John's declared a national harbour? I understand provision was made in the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada to provide the province with one national harbour.
