410. Administration, operation and maintenance including fees for membership in the international organizations listed in the details of the estimates, $6,015,938.

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to take the minister for a relaxing cruise for two or three minutes around some of the Kootenay lakes and rivers. I want to say, first of all, that the people of my district appreciate very much the improvements which have been made in recent years-I am going back now some five or six years- to the aids to navigation on the lakes and rivers in the district.
Prior to that time, in many cases the aids to navigation were somewhat limited. In some cases you just had a five gallon oil can tacked on to a stump and the pilot would steer for that, and then a little further up the river he would steer for somebody's outdoor convenience, and that sort of thing. However, there has been a big improvement. There have been a number of rocks and bars marked which have been hazards to navigation throughout the years.
However, I rise to draw the attention of the minister to the rapid increase in the amount of water traffic on the Columbia river, the Arrow lakes and the Kootenay lakes for two reasons in particular. The
Supply-Transport
first is the very rapid expansion in the lumber industry which has caused the use of a much larger number of tugs which draw more water, generally speaking, than the stern-wheelers did and which are liable to run aground on some of the sand bars which the sternwheelers slid over. Then there has been a greater use of barges handling materials, etc., used in connection with lumber camps, and in addition the growing use of booms of a new type. We are changing from the bag boom as I have known it since I was a boy to some other sort of boom that draws six or eight feet of water. They are tied with steel bands. On account of this change in the type of boats using the lakes and rivers, additional marking is required.
Furthermore, there is an urgent need for additional markings because of the great increase which has taken place in the number of pleasure craft. One of the hazards connected with these craft is the speed at which they travel. A boat moving at nine or ten knots could go aground on a bar without too much damage being caused, but when you are travelling at 30 or 40 miles an hour it does not take much of a bar to throw you into the lake. There has been a tremendous increase in the number of pleasure craft being used locally, and there has also been a surprising increase in the number which come from the United States, either by way of the Columbia river or through the Kootenay river into the Kootenay lakes. In many cases their owners spend a few days on the Kootenay lakes, then go over to the Columbia river or the Arrow lakes, or vice versa. This traffic now comes from as far south as Portland. My own son-in-law counted 22 such craft during the last Labour day week end which had come from Portland, Oregon. They now have low-boys so that they can get these craft up past the dams so as to proceed up the river. I have heard officers of yacht clubs south of the boundary say that our Kootenay lakes and river system offered such delightful conditions for holidays that these people are coming in ever increasing numbers. So we need to do more marking on the river.
I suggest that the minister should give consideration to marking the river between Arrowhead and Revelstoke. Five cruisers which came up the river on Labour day week end last year broke their propellers against obstacles in this section of the channel. Then there is the necessity for marking some bars which have so far remained unmarked in the Arrow lakes. Local residents know where these hazards are. They are only two or three feet below the surface of the water at low water. The old-time tugboat captains knew where they were, but now you have these

Supply-Transport
pleasure craft coming up from the States and there is a great risk of serious accident. I would ask the minister to check for the need for more markers in the Arrow lakes a mile or two south of Arrowhead. One of the sand bars which is unmarked is less than two feet below the surface at extremely low water, and there is another rock hazard at about the same depth.
In addition, I suggest there should be careful supervision over the buoys in the narrows between the upper and lower Arrow lakes. These buoys are anchored to their sites, but some of them get torn away at high water. In some cases they have not been replaced. Unless something is done about it a number of these pleasure craft will probably run ashore on sand bars. I suggest that this section of the river be checked very closely and also the aids to navigation between Castlegar and the international boundary. There is some very swift water there and I suggest consideration be given to placing some prominent sign this side of the international boundary south of Fort Shepphard-or Waneta-which would indicate that craft must go to the easterly side of the water to get away from some dangerous rapids. What has been done is excellent, and is quite sufficient for those persons from local boat clubs, and even some of those from Spokane who have travelled the river a number of times, but I notice that increasingly people coming into the Arrow lakes do so without any prior knowledge of the river or the narrows, and I marvel that there are not more accidents. I bring these few matters to the attention of the minister, and suggest he should ask his officials to check them very carefully because there is going to be a tremendous increase in water traffic.
There is one other matter I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. I understand, of course, that the preparation of charts comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, but I repeatedly get requests for a chart of this river from the international boundary onward. I understand that consideration was given to preparation of one last year by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, but they were loaded with work and unable to complete it. I suggest that a chart is very necessary. Its publication should not involve any public expenditure. It could be sold readily at a dollar at the international boundary, or at Trail, and should be available to local people who are interested in navigation on these waters. Thus its cost to the treasury could readily be recovered.
That is all I have to say at the present time.

We are very glad to have reports at any time telling us if any buoys or markings are missing. We would like to have that information as soon as we can. We welcome these reports, and if the hon. member or the people in his area would tell us the location of any of these obstacles which were mentioned this afternoon we should be glad to take on the task of seeing that they are properly marked.

May I say while we are on this subject that I should like to compliment the department in connection with the navigational aids I saw last year on a trip to the northern waters of the Athabasca. I had occasion to travel on that route to the north, and I was impressed by the efficiency of the system.
I have travelled northern waters for years and spent many a night on a gravel bar. I think the navigational aids which have been provided by the department has made traffic much easier and I suggest the minister give consideration to supplying similar aids on the Peace river. There is not the commercial traffic on the river that there was many years ago, but there is an increasing number of pleasure boats and I think it would be of great assistance to people using the river in this way. It is so easy now to navigate that I think any hon. member would be able to keep off the shoals and gravel bars.
I have one further comment to make but before doing so I should like to ask the minister if he can assure the committee that it is the intention of his department to keep up this work, to supply navigational aids, and to keep navigation open even from the farthest south port of Fort McMurray to the north, and to continue this service?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I am glad to assure the hon. member that we not only intend to keep up this service but to improve it where we can.

I am glad to hear that, Mr. Chairman, because last year when I appeared before the Manning commission I heard statements made by the railway companies and other parties who advocated the eastern route for a railway north to Slave lake. These were predicated on the belief that navigation services from Fort McMurray to Uranium City were going to be closed out thus leaving the traffic free for the railway companies. They would then be in a position to proceed without any competition.
The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour recently returned from a visit to Uranium City and knows the difficulties confronting those people. They have relied upon the use of the Athabaska river system from

Fort McMurray into lake Athabaska to provide a safe, effective and reasonably cheap service to carry their in-bound traffic. The figures quoted by the railway companies indicated that a sum in the neighbourhood of $500,000 would be added to the charges on freight going into the Uranium City area, if the railway were built on the east route. As long as it appears that the lower reaches of the Athabaska river will be kept open, the people in that sorely pressed area will look forward to receiving their freight at a reasonable charge.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question at this time. Are some improvements to be made to aids to navigation at lake Winnipeg this season? Also what steps have been taken to re-establish the Selkirk subagency?

Mr. Chairman, the answer to
the first part of the hon. member's question is yes. The whole question of subagencies is now under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, the minister and his officials will have received representations from fishermen about my question. Many west coast fishermen have purchased equipment for use with the Loran system of navigation, the short form for the long range navigation system. I believe there were two Loran stations on the west coast and it was hoped additional ones would be established in order that the fishermen with the sets could use them. I understand that another system called the Decca system was developed in England. It operates substantially the same way. I believe experiments with it were conducted on the west coast a few months ago. I should like to know how it is working out and what is the intention of the department with reference to establishing additional long range navigation stations on the west coast for use by fishermen.
There are splendid aids to navigation off the southern part of the coast of British Columbia north of the strait of Georgia, up through Johnstone strait and the inlets below cape Caution, and between Vancouver island and the mainland. There are insufficient aids to navigation including spar buoys, bell buoys, lights, etc. off the upper or northern coast of the province. Perhaps the larger volume of traffic operating off the coast of the southern mainland explains the situation. The department has been extremely kind in the past in meeting requests for additional aids to navigation and I would request that consideration be given to the provision of additional aids off the coast of the northern mainland.
Supply-Transport
With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I wish to refer to a problem that falls under the divided jurisdiction of the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works. 1 have engaged in extensive correspondence with the hydrographic branch and with the Department of Public Works with reference to the dredging of the Metlakatla bar off the coast of Prince Rupert and I disagree, as do many Prince Rupert fishermen, with the decision of the government not to proceed with the dredging of this bar. This project plus additional aids to navigation would be of great assistance to fishermen in that area. They can cross the bar from half flood through to half ebb tide but when it is below ebb tide the bar is too high and there is not sufficient water to allow passage. Boats either have to wait or travel some distance to the south and take another entrance to the harbour of Prince Rupert.
Will the minister indicate to me and to the committee the working conditions, or the conditions of employment, of lighthouse keepers and tenders and people who work at lighthouses; their hours of work, their time off, and so forth; how much time they are required to spend as a lighthouse tender before they get to be a keeper, and so forth?
I notice on page 519 of the details something which seems rather odd. Perhaps the minister can give an explanation of this also. About the eighth or tenth item from the bottom there is a classification of moulder helper and patternmaker. I assume from the reference here that this classification is the type of work involved in making castings of different metals for different purposes. I do not know whether that is so or not, but I am sure that would be the designation that a patternmaker would have in making patterns for castings. I would assume the moulder helper would work in that capacity also. I wonder why there is no moulder involved? What are the functions and duties of those two particular classes?

Regarding the placing of navigational aids, every year representatives of my department meet with various marine organizations in the areas and discuss with them what is needed. Then to the very best of our ability we try to carry out the wishes expressed.
With regard to what we are doing in the area represented by the hon. member, the Prince Rupert agency has specific items and I shall be glad to show them to the hon. member if he wishes to see all the details. We have an expenditure during this year of about $100,000.
Regarding the salaries and working conditions of lighthouse keepers, while I was

Supply-Transport
visiting Prince Rupert three years ago, a visit to which the hon. member kindly referred a while ago, I went out on the Alexander Mackenzie to visit various lighthouses and lighthouse keepers. I think that lighthouse keepers are about the happiest group of people that you will find anywhere. Ours appear to be very happy in their jobs. I should like to assure him that their salaries and conditions of work are under constant review. I believe he will find on talking to them that they are pleased and satisfied with their jobs at the present time.
Regarding the employees to whom the hon. member referred, the moulder helper and the patternmaker, at our marine agencies we have a carpenter shop and a blacksmith shop, and naturally it might look strange if there is a moulder helper when there is no moulder. I am advised that is the strange way the civil service commission writes up these particular positions. I agree with him that these particular classifications are puzzling at times I assure him the employees of these marine agencies on these jobs are able to do the work that is asked of them.

I appreciate the minister's feeling and attitude toward lighthouse keepers. Sometimes you cannot get all the comments. The microphone is very sensitive. I heard some reference to the fact that the lighthouse keepers' salaries are under constant review; that they are happy, contented and so on. That is not the question I asked. I asked what are the working conditions; how much time do they spend in the lighthouse or at any particular lighthouse before relief for them is obtained, and things of that general nature? What specific conditions of employment apply to lighthouse keepers, and not whether they are contented and happy, was my question.
I had some difficulty in getting my hearing aid to function properly, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps the minister mentioned this; if so, I did not get it and I apologize, but I did make some query as to what is transpiring with respect to long range navigational systems. If the minister mentioned that I did not hear him and I apologize and I would appreciate it if he would reiterate it. If he did not mention it, perhaps he will tell me exactly what is happening in that regard.
Third, if under the present classification someone is classified as a helper but is not a helper, then certainly the civil service commission should change the classification. If he is performing the duties and functions and carrying out the responsibilities that a moulder, which is a craft and trade, has to carry out, then I am of the opinion that on

a salary of $2,870 a year he is grossly underpaid. Even as a helper he is grossly underpaid at that rate.

Regarding the working conditions, salaries, and so on, of lighthouse keepers, those are classified positions which come under the civil service commission and all those details are worked out by the commission. I will be very glad to get the details for the hon. member and let him have them as soon as I am able to obtain them.
Regarding the installation of additional Loran installations, these, as the hon. member knows, are very expensive indeed and the question of additional installations is now under very active study.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is some reference in this vote to membership fees in international organizations listed in the details on page 518. I am not able to find those international organizations. I doubt whether they are listed on page 518. Will the minister put the organizations on Hansard?
Yes, I have them right here. The international association of lighthouse authorities, $439; the permanent international association of navigational congresses, $200; these are the only two.

I should like to get some information from the minister with regard to some of the inland lakes in the northern part of our provinces, particularly in northern Manitoba, respecting aids to navigation. Each year we see an increasing number of pleasure craft on those lakes. I am wondering whether there is any obligation on the Department of Transport to provide reef marks on those large northern lakes, or whether there is any financial assistance available to various groups such as campers' associations, and so on, to mark those reefs so that they make the lakes safe for navigation?
Yes, Mr. Chairman. We mark the reefs when charts have been made of the lakes, and charts are made by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys when there is demand for them.

Just one brief question on that explanation. For instance, in my opinion some of the lakes in that area should be classified as navigable waters. What is the explanation of the term "navigable waters", so far as the Department of Transport is concerned?

It is not a question of whether or not the waters are navigable, it is a question of whether any commercial use of any importance is made of the waters. If there is,

then there are charts made and the reefs are marked. If the hon. member could bring specific lakes, specific waters, to our attention we would certainly have a look into such cases.

I wanted some information on the contract services for lake Superior. The details are on page 520 of the book of estimates. There was $75,000 last year, and nothing is to be spent this year. Does this mean that the amount last year was just for the icebreaker services?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, this was the contract price for the icebreaker tug which we employed last year before we built our own icebreaker. There is no figure for this year because the icebreaking is being done by our own vessel.

I wanted to bring up another matter in connection with the lake Superior services and this relates to the situation at Nipigon. There is every promise that Nipigon may develop into an ore shipping point, although this may be some time in the future. We have a most complicated transportation situation at Nipigon. We have the harbour, which is rather small, and which is dredged by the Department of Public Works; the Ontario department of highways has a bridge over the river very close to the harbour, and we have the Canadian National Railways bridge over the river which is also close to the harbour. We have the Nipigon river, which is a stream emptying into lake Superior and which carries a great deal of pulpwood. I believe there is more pulpwood carried on this river than any other river in Canada. The Department of Public Works has spent money in the past in building up the retaining walls along the river as it goes out into the harbour area.
The residents in the town have informed me that their worries in connection with this particular river and harbour came to a head last August when they had a flood there which led to the crumbling of some of the embankment. I have made requests of the Department of Public Works to examine the situation and make sure that every step has been taken to protect the embankment there. I wonder if the minister could explain to me what role his department plays in interrelating the development and the safety of a harbour such as Nipigon which is so complicated with all these other transportation authorities having an interest in having a good safe harbour, a good safe river, and no danger of any embankment sliding into the stream or into the harbour.

Mr. Chairman, we work out these various problems in close consultation with
Supply-Transport
the Department of Public Works. It is a joint operation and whenever a situation like this arises the two departments get together and do the best they can.

Could I make a request of the minister that he check with the Department of Public Works to see what they have done in this regard and make absolutely sure of the future safety of the community and the future safety of the harbour in terms of silting up or of any breakaways from the bank, and to see that the situation is examined by some kind of engineering team so that some kind of report can be made available both to the departments and to the people in the area?

I am advised that the Department of Public Works will consult us if they feel navigation is involved. Any time we are asked to work with them on matters of this kind or are advised of a situation of this kind we will be glad to look at it in conjunction with the public works department.

There has been mention by one or two members of overlapping between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport. This moves me to ask a question which I had forgotten to ask previously at the request of some of the people of my constituency, particularly those interested in using wharves, lumbering, and things of that sort. Apparently the Department of Transport is in the habit, in outlying places, of appointing permanent employees or officials of the Department of Public Works as their agents.
Now, the first question I want to ask is, are they agents of the Department of Transport at all times or only at such times as they are rendering services for which the Department of Transport is responsible? My second question is, does the Department of Transport accept full responsibility for the actions of agents appointed by them who are officials of the Department of Public Works?
If they are performing functions for us, then we are responsible for their activities and they are agents of ours.
My other question was, are they agents of the Department of Transport at all times, as it were?
No, only when they are performing specific tasks for us.

Then during this time the department accepts responsibility for their actions?

Private Bills-Divorce
It is a matter of function; it is not a matter of time. If they are doing a job for us as our agents we accept responsibility for what they do.

I wanted to follow up this line of discussion I had with the minister a moment ago. I am sorry it got off on something else, but it had to do with the long range navigational aids. The minister indicated, and I think his words were, that this was under active study or active consideration and that plans were in the offing for establishing a system of that nature.
I should like to correct that. I did not say plans were in the offing. I said the matter was under study.

I am perhaps adding words that the minister did not use, and I apologize for that. The question is under study. I know it has been under study for quite some time, and I know there is a conflict as between types or systems of aids to navigation, some developed in the United States and some developed in other countries.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order; it being five o'clock, in order to allow the house to proceed to the consideration of private and public bills it is my duty, pursuant to section 3 of standing order 15, to rise, report certain resolutions, and request leave to sit again later this day or the next sitting of the house as the case may be.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.
The house in committee on Bill No. SD-50, for the relief of Rose Vosko Ribkoff-Mr. McCleave-Mr. Rea in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall we take the 45 divorce bills under one item?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Then the committee will consider Bill No. SD-50.
On Clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The bill we have before us is report 59 of the Senate. This is probably what we, after our long experience in debating these bills, would call a very stereotyped divorce case in which it would appear from reading the evidence that it was a framed case, that the evidence we are discussing was not necessarily the evidence that was involved in this particular case but that it was a common television type of divorce case. Unfortunately or fortunately it 

affects some extremely young people. The clerk of the committee established the following information:
By the Clerk of the Committee:
Q. What is your name?
A. Rose Ribkoff.
Q. What is your age?
A. Twenty five.
Q. Where do you live?
A. Montreal.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Bookkeeper.
Q. Are you married and if so to whom?
A. I am married to Irving Ribkoff.
Q. When were you married?
A. March 13, 1954.
Q. Where?
A. In. Plattsburg, New York.
Q. In Plattsburg or Glens Falls?
A. I was married in Plattsburg.

Mr. Chairman, there is an error as to the year of the marriage. I would ask that paragraph one be amended to correspond to the marriage certificate, as being the 13th day of March, 1954 instead of 1953.
This may have been a Friday. If it was, it was probably not too good a day because it would appear, just from reading this evidence and from drawing an inference, that this young girl, at that time only 19 years of age, on Friday the 13th, went down to the United States and got married probably without her parents' consent. At any rate, the marriage took place as proved by a document that was presented, namely the marriage certificate which was filed and marked as exhibit No. 1. A photograph taken two and a half years ago is presented as exhibit No. 2. This is a likeness of the husband of the petitioner. Mr. Jacobs, an advocate from Montreal I believe, appeared as counsel for the petitioner and began his questioning as follows:
By Mr. Jacobs:
Q. Mrs. Ribkoff, where was your husband born?
A. In Montreal.
Q. Where has he resided during his life time?
A. In Montreal.
Q. During your marriage with him what city did you live in?
A. In Montreal.
But they did get married in the United States. The questioning continues:
Q. To your knowledge where is your husband living today?
A. In Montreal.
Q. Did you have any children with your husband?
A. Yes, I have.
Q. How many?
A. Two.
Q. What are their names and how old are they?
A. Arlene Adele is 5, born October 18, 1954; and Stephen Warren, 3, bom August 24, 1956.
It may be interesting, Mr. Chairman, to go back and check with the marriage certificate because there is some doubt whether they got married in 1953 or 1954. At any rate the questioning continues as follows:

Q. During your marriage with your husband could you tell us how you got along with him?
A. Not very well.
Q. What trouble did you have?
A. He beat me, he insulted me, he was abusive, spoke harshly, came home late.
Q. How late would he come home?
A. Three and four a.m.
Q. How often?
A. Almost every night.
Q. Did you speak to him about his conduct?
A. Yes, I did.
Q. What was his reply?
A. He said that it was none of my business.
Q. As a result of the facts you have stated did anything happen to you in April 1957?
A. Yes, I became ill.
Q. What type of illness did you contract?
A. Tuberculosis.
Q. As a result of that illness did you spend any time in the sanitarium?
A. Yes, I did.
Q. How long were you there?
A. Ten and a half months.
Q. During this period of time who looked after the children?
A. My mother did.
Q. Do you remember your husband coming to see you in the sanitarium in January 1958?
A. Yes, I do.
Q. Did you have any discussion with him?
A. 1 did.
Q. What did he tell you at that time?
A. I told him I was to be discharged the following month and that we would require a home in Montreal, and he says as far as he is concerned it is my problem not his because he has no intention of setting up home for me like that.
Q. Were you discharged the following month?
A. Yes, I was.
Q. February 1958?
A. Yes.
Q. Where did you have to go?
A. To my mother's.
Q. Since that time has he ever set up a home for you?
A. No, he has not.
Q. Did you do your own part, did you make any attempt to try to bring the family together?
A. Yes, I did, because my mother's house was too small and I felt I wanted to take an apartment with my husband and try to make a go of our marriage.
Q. Did that ever work out?
A. No, he refused.
If we go back to the real reason, Mr. Chairman, why this marriage did not succeed or why the parties did not get along, what do we find? I have not been able to find out how old the husband is. She was 19 years old when she got married. I am not sure how old the husband was. I am not really sure why Mr. Jacobs changed the date on the marriage certificate. But if the new date was correct instead of the old one, the petitioner got off to a bad start in the first place because of the situation existing and probably there was a terrific amount of resentment involved in this marriage. What we are about to find out as to the grounds for the adultery charge in this case is not necessarily important to the case at all but it has incidentally arisen out of the fact that the husband resented the marriage in the first place and
Private Bills-Divorce
that the arrangements did not work out. The second child followed the first. The stay in the sanitarium did not help the situation at all so that by the time she was ready to leave the sanitarium the husband had decided that he had no intention and certainly no desire to set up a house for his wife. Senator Roebuck continues with the questioning and he is interested in ascertaining whether any arrangements had been made for financial support, particularly in view of the fact that the husband has already indicated that he has no intention of renting an apartment.
By the Chairman (Senator Roebuck):
Q. Did he give you any money for the support of yourself and the children?
A. Yes.
Q. How much?
A. Not very much.
By Mr. Jacobs:
Q. How much weekly, actually?
A. $20 a week.
Q. As a matter of fact, by court order is he now contributing $25 a week for the support of you and the children?
A. Yes.
Q. And you have sufficiently regained your health and I understand you are engaged as a bookkeeper?
A. That is right.
Q. And the children live with you?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you have anyone looking after them while you work?
A. Yes, I have an efficient housekeeper.
By Senator Lambert:
Q. Do these payments come in regularly?
A. Yes.
By Mr. Jacobs:
Q. Do you have any personal knowledge of your husband's alleged adultery on March 3, 1959 at the Croyden apartment hotel in Montreal?
A. I was informed by the detectives.
Q. But you were not present at the time?
A. No.
Q. Is there any collusion or arrangement between you and your husband to obtain this divorce?
A. No.
Q. Have you in any way connived with anyone to bring this petition before the committee today?
A. No.
Q. Has there been any condonement or forgiveness on your part?
A. No.
Q. Would you take him back today?
A. No.
Mr. Chairman, these questions must be asked but it would seem to me that we are only asking people to lie and to perjure themselves for no particular good reason. We are all aware, I am sure, on reading this evidence that the wife is not paying for this petition, that she has no money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: How do you know?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have read the bill. Have you? We have no indication whether the evidence proves that or not. If the hon. member wishes to make comments I would like to see him rise-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It would appear to me that the wife is receiving for herself and her two children the princely sum of $25 a week under a court order. Out of this amount we are being asked to believe that she has been able to save enough money to obtain this divorce, a divorce which costs on the average around $2,500. It would seem to me that this woman has not enough money to live on as it is and would certainly not have much money to pay for a divorce.
If we come to that conclusion, then we must also come to the conclusion that she is going to a get a divorce because her husband is willing to pay for that divorce, and if he is willing to pay for the divorce 1 think we can draw the further conclusion that he has already arranged another alliance for himself and wishes the divorce in order to marry somebody else. This is the deduction which has been proved by a young lady who makes a living doing this kind of thing-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I think we are safe in saying that in this particular case it is probably the husband who wants the divorce more than the wife. The amount of money indicated in the evidence which the woman has is not sufficient to allow her to get a divorce, pay for the lawyers and the other costs involved.
Senator Roebuck continues the questioning as follows:
Q. Did you ever discuss the question with your husband about his actions on March 3, 1959?
A. No.
Q. When did you have your last marital relations with your husband?
A. When the baby was conceived, when Stephen Warren was conceived.
Q. That would be some nine months prior to August 24. Well, at all events, since March 3, 1959 have you had any relations with your husband of that kind?
A. No.
Then Peter Rosen appeared as a witness on behalf of the petitioner, and having been duly sworn testified as follows. We have heard of Mr. Rosen before. He lives in Montreal and classes himself as an investigator. He is questioned by Mr. Jacobs as follows:
Q. I am showing you a photograph which has been filed as exhibit 2, can you identify the man in the picture?
A. That is Mr. Israel Ribkoff.
Q. Did you have occasion to investigate the conduct of Mr. Israel Ribkoff or Irving Ribkoff?
A. Yes, I did.
Q. What did you ascertain?
A. I saw Mr. Ribkoff on several occasions at the time when he visited his wife's home on Ellendale, and learned he had a four door car, black, licence number 217178; and I also found he stayed at the Croyden apartment hotel on Cote des Neiges road; he was staying in room 720 at the time. On March 3, 1959 I followed him that

day and he arrived at the corner of Peel and Sherbrooke streets and he met this young lady and he picked her up, she was waiting for him at the corner, and they drove to a restaurant on Decarie boulevard circle, to the restaurant Ruby Foo's, and they were there about an hour and a half; they then came out and they drove back to Mr. Ribkoff's apartment, the Croyden apartments on Cote des Neiges road, and they both came out of the car.
Mr. Chairman, is this not exactly what we are told happened in this type of case not long ago in another connection? The young lady working in these cases does not come to the apartment. She wants to meet in a restaurant so that they can have a cup of coffee and talk the matter over so it is all on the up and up. This is what happened in this particular case. She is waiting on a street corner, not at her home. You will remember that many times on returning home they were left on a street corner so that the people on the street they live on do not know they are being driven home every night by a different man. In this case she is picked up on the street corner and driven to a restaurant, a fairly respectable restaurant I presume.
The evidence continues:
Mr. Ribkoff locked both doors of the car, and they both went into the building. I followed them in, and they went up to the apartment 720 and they both went inside and the door was shut. I waited around a few minutes, and I then went down to the lobby and I used a pay phone there to call my man. As a result of the call my man met me there shortly before 11.30 and together we went back up to the room 720. I rang the bell.
Mr. Chairman, I think all stationery stores should be really angry at the turn of events taking place in these divorce cases recently. Before we always had them putting adhesive tape or some other kind of tape on the door, but now they do not bother. From the number of cases we have read before it must have been a very profitable business for stationery stores and I think they should in all fairness spread the money around which they get out of this and that they should follow the previous practice. It was so phony it sounded plausible.
This is a very stereotyped sort of case and you can know almost what is in it without reading it; but there are small differences in the evidence and I should read it. The questioning is continued by the chairman of the other place, Senator Roebuck, as foRows:
Q. What time was this?
A. That was shortly after 11.30. We went up to the apartment and I rang the bell. It took a few minutes and a man came to the door, and as he opened the door we pushed our way into the room. The man started to yell at us and wanted to know what business we had coming in there.
Mr. Golden, my man, quietened him down-
It does not say so here but they probably twisted his arm or something.

-and I showed him this photograph I had, exhibit 2, and asked him if that was his picture and if he was Israel Ribkoff. He admitted that it was his picture, that he was Israel Ribkoff. He wanted to know what it was all about. I told him we were acting on behalf of his wife. We looked around, it is one large room, continental bed there, with two pillows on it, and the bed was disarranged, but we didn't see anybody else. So 1 asked him, "Where is the woman you came into the apartment with?" He said, "What do you need her for?" I said, "We want to speak to her." So we tried the door, which was a bathroom door, and it was locked, and she was in the bathroom.
They not only knocked on the bathroom but this is what they did:
So I knocked on the door, and she wouldn't come out, so I said, "You had better come out, lady, or we will break the door." So Mr. Ribkoff spoke to her through the door and she asked him to give her something. He handed her something, I think it was a slip through the bathroom door, and she opened up and came out a few minutes later dressed in a slip: and I asked her for her name and address, and she at first didn't want to but I told her I would check it and find out where she lived, she told me then that her name was Mliss Jean Hill and she lived at 5705 Westminster Avenue.
Here again is another of these cases where the people have no respect whatsoever for privacy of any description. They tell a young lady that if she does not come out of the bathroom they will break the door down and come in. I would be very surprised if these people could get away with this type of action and still have the licence or the privilege to call themselves investigators. They quietened the man in this case. I do not know how. They may have used force on him. Then they go on to force this young lady to come out of the bathroom by telling her that if she does not they will break the door down.
By Mr. Jacobs:
Q. Did you notice any clothing around the room?
A. Yes, women's clothing on the chair near the bed, and some man's underclothing and a shirt and tie on another chair in the room.
Q. There was no doubt in your mind the bed had been occupied by two people?
A. No, definitely it was pretty well mussed up, what we saw.
I draw your attention particularly, Mr. Chairman, to that last question and to the reply which was given. I suggest that that question could never be answered in the affirmative. The reply to that question would always be an expression of opinion. Unless two people were in the bed it could not definitely be said that two people had occupied that bed. Anything else would be an expression of opinion by the witness.
Next, Abe Golden appeared as a witness on behalf of the petitioner, gave his age as 52, his address as Montreal and stated he considers himself to be an investigator. Mr. Jacobs asked him questions, to which he gave answers as follows:

Q. I show you a photograph which has been filed as exhibit 2, can you identify the man in that picture?
A. Mr. Israel Ribkoff.
Q. Were you with Mr. Rosen on the evening of March 3, 1959?
A. Yes sir.
Q. When you saw Mr. Israel Ribkoff?
A. Yes sir.
Q. Tell us under what circumstances and where?
A. Room 720 at the Croyden hotel, on Cote des Neiges. We entered the room. Mr. Ribkoff was in the room number 720. All he had on was his trousers. There was just a continental bed which was used, and we saw no woman, and Mr. Rosen went over to the bathroom door and knocked on the door, and we tried to get the woman out, and she wouldn't come out; she hollered out of the bathroom, "Throw me something Iz." So he threw her slip in, and she comes out, this woman, wearing the slip. Mr. Rosen asked her her name, and she didn't want to give it at first, but then she said, "Jean Hill". Mr. Ribkoff asked us to leave the room, so we left-didn't want to argue with him.
Q. What was the condition of the bed in that room?
A. The bed was disturbed.
Q. How many beds?
A. One continental bed, double bed.
By the Chairman (Senator Roebuck):
Q. Did the bed show signs of two people having been in it?
A. Yes, gentlemen.
Q. It showed signs of having been slept in?
A. Yes, gentlemen.
By Senator Golding:
Q. Was that the only time you were on the case?
A. Yes, sir.
On application by Mr. Jacobs, the name "Irving Ribkoff" was amended to read "Israel (Irving) Ribkoff", wherever the said name appears on the petition. Amendment granted.
This is one of those cases that is as phoney as a three dollar bill. There is no doubt in my mind that this evidence could easily have been manufactured. There is no real evidence that intercourse had taken place at all, and if it had not taken place, then obviously there can be no support of a charge of adultery and until there is some proof or indication that intercourse did take place, then there is no adultery.
I suggest we cannot pass this bill on the ground in the petition which said definitely that adultery had taken place. It is not good enough to say adultery could have taken place, or that it is possible for it to take place. I am sure it is possible that adultery can take place at any time and in almost any place, but that does not necessarily mean to say it does and just because there is an opportunity is no reason in my opinion for any consideration to be given to this objection. This case in particular is based on very limited and stereotyped evidence. As a matter of fact there is not enough evidence here for a decent discussion of the problem. The bill itself reads as follows:
Whereas Rose Vosko Ribkoff, residing at the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec, wife of Israel (Irving) Ribkoff, who is domiciled in

Private Bills-Divorce
Canada and residing at the city of Quebec, in the said province, has by her petition alleged that they were married on the thirteenth day of March, A.D. 1954, at the town of Plattsburg, in the state of New York, one of the United States of America, she then being Hose Vosko; and whereas by her petition she has prayed that, on the ground of adultery since then, their marriage be dissolved; and whereas the said marriage and adultery have been proved by evidence adduced and it is expedient that the prayer of her petition be granted: Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
The said marriage is hereby dissolved, and shall be henceforth null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever.
It says here: "the said marriage and adultery have been proved by evidence."
I suggest that the marriage has been proved, but I strongly maintain that the charge of adultery has not been proved, and this is the only type of evidence which can be accepted. If we want to say we will grant this divorce because we think the man has a new girl friend he wants to marry, or because we think the petitioner has a boy friend she wants to marry, very good. I think we should grant the divorce, and that these are sufficient grounds. But I maintain strongly that if we are going to say in the bill that adultery has been proved then that is not a fact. We are drawing an implication so broad that it becomes ridiculous. This is one of those stereotyped cases that the lawyers have developed of a kind which is meeting with considerable success in the other house and which should receive very close scrutiny by hon. members here. We should not ask people to come before us or the other house with evidence of this nature and ask for relief on this type of testimony.
Mr Howard: Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments to make-
Blocking and more blocking.

I beg your pardon? Mr. Chairman, I do not know if the hon. member was relieving himself of a political platitude or if he had some comment to make and that is why I begged his pardon.
I am disturbed about one aspect of this case which has cropped up time and time again in these cases, the means by which investigators obtain their evidence. People just do not allow complete strangers to walk into their homes at late hours and finding them in a state of partial or complete undress interrogate them about these personal matters.
Mr. Rosen, the first investigator to testify in this instance is probably more honest than his partner and many other investigators because he explains how he gained entry to

the room. Let me read his evidence at this point. At page 12 he is questioned by Senator Roebuck as follows:
Q. What time was this?
A. That was shortly after 11.30. We went up to the apartment and I rang the bell. It took a few minutes, and a man came to the door,-
This is the relevant part:
-and as he opened the door we pushed our way into the room.
This is how most investigators gain entry. They push their way into homes disregarding people's rights. They barge in trampling the rights of the individuals.
Someone snickers in an awkward, nasty way at my reference to people's rights indicating that they do not have any.
Indicating that you do not acknowledge them.
That is the blatant answer we get indicating that I do not acknowledge their rights.
That is correct.
That is precisely the point I am getting at. I am acknowledging the rights of these individuals to their privacy. I suggest the manner in which the divorce laws are drawn-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I cannot allow the hon. member to discuss a matter of procedure and he will have to come back to the bill.

In order to meet the test under the rules of the other place governing divorce the rights of individuals are trampled upon. This is what happens in complete disregard of the rights of those individuals to privacy. Mr. Rosen indicates that there was objection on the part of the respondent to the invasion of his apartment. I continue:
The man started to yell at us and wanted to know what business we had coming in there.
The man objected to the forced entry of these two strangers at this late hour and was justified in doing so because he did not know them and there was no conversation. They forced their way in thereby invading the rights of the individual to his privacy and contravening the Criminal Code with respect to trespass and possibly with respect to assault. This is the impression I am given by members of the bar who have much more knowledge of these matters than I have.
As though he were referring to Robinson Crusoe, Mr. Rosen goes on to state:
Mr. Golden, my man, quieted him down-
We do not know how this was accomplished, whether by persuasive talk or threats of physical violence. I contend that the

investigator used threats of additional trespass, assault and damage to property. About inquiring where the corespondent was, Mr. Rosen stated:
So I asked him, "Where is the woman you came into the apartment with?" He said, "What do you need her for?"
That may be classified as hearsay and not admissible, but in any event that is what he said. I continue:
I said, "We want to speak to her." So we tried the door, which was a bathroom door, and it was locked, and she was in the bathroom. So I knocked on the door, and she wouldn't come out, so I said, "You had better come out, lady, or we will break the door."
As in previous cases we have here the evidence of an investigator to the effect that he violated the privacy of an individual and contravened the provisions of the Criminal Code with respect to trespass and later on with respect to threats of property damage and further trespass and assault.
It is accepted certainly by us here as being the normal thing which occurs; it is accepted generally by society. I think it is accepted-I do not think it should be-because we probably all realize that in these circumstances this was the method that had to be used by the investigators to gain this particular evidence; otherwise, they might not have obtained it and we might not have the case before us. These people are employed as investigators to work on behalf of the petitioner. They knew from their past experience that they had to discover certain things in order to appear before parliament and give evidence with respect to those things.
They go on to talk about the state of the clothing and the state of the bed, whether it was a single or a double bed, and so on. But we have come to accept here-I think unfortunately-the fact that in some instances the rights of people have to be violated; that the Criminal Code has to be violated; that trespass has to be indulged in; that sometimes physical violence has to be indulged in and, as indicated in other cases, sometimes threats have to be made, assault has to be carried out in order to obtain this sort of evidence. Yet we all know, Mr. Chairman, that under other circumstances if this were to occur and it did not occur in conjunction with a court case, or it was done by someone who did not have a search warrant, immediately there would be charges laid against the individuals involved in trespass, assault, theft or whatever else arose out of the activities of the individuals in the case.
It is regrettable that we have come to forget that those rights do exist in society, at least we have forgotten them in so far as
79951-0-285J

divorce cases are concerned. We wink our eyes at them or say to ourselves: Because the law insists that manufactured evidence be developed, insists that hyprocrisy be the rule of the day, we also shut our eyes to other violations of such rights and practices. In this case there was the pushing of their way into the room and threats to knock down the door if a certain thing were not agreed to. We say, "Well, this is all right and we will content ourselves to let it pass." Let us forget it and not look at the fact that there was an invasion of privacy and there were violations of the Criminal Code to obtain the evidence, because we know that the law itself relating to adultery is crazy in the first place and insists upon this sort of activity to provide the grounds for divorce.
I should refer to the circumstances in order to give the entire picture. Evidence was given by Mr. Golden, another investigator. He also relates his activities, starting at page 13, from which I am reading now. He was questioned by Mr. Jacobs as follows:
Q. Tell us under what circumstances and where?
This was in relation to when he saw the defendant. I continue:
A. Room No.-at the-on Cote des Neiges.
All that he says, Mr. Chairman, is that they entered the room. We recall this, Mr. Chairman, the door was open, as a matter of fact, and they entered. He makes no reference to the pushing of their way into the room, no reference to the man starting to yell at them, no reference to his own participation, as given by Mr. Rosen. Perhaps I should clear this up. Mr. Rosen said that the respondent started to yell at them, wanted to know what business they had and Mr. Golden-that is the other investigator- quietened him down. When Mr. Golden comes in to give his account of what occurred, the circumstances, and where this occurred, he makes no reference to his quietening anybody down or if he did how he did it; no reference to their manner of entry into the apartment, no reference to what the respondent said at that stage of entering the door, only the words "we entered the room". That was all.
Then he gives an account of what the respondent was wearing, the bed that was there, the condition it was in, and so on. Yet he does not incriminate his own partner with respect to what Mr. Rosen said. He said to the lady in the bathroom-and you will recall, Mr. Chairman, Mr. Rosen said, "You had better come out, lady, or we will break the door". His partner says that Mr. Rosen went over to the bathroom door and knocked on the door. He said, "We tried to get the woman out and she would not come out". She hollered out of the bathroom "Throw me'

Private Bills-Divorce
something". He was referring to the respondent, and then he indicates that he threw her slip in and she came out wearing her slip.
If in the first instance I over-emphasized this question of invasion of rights of the citizen, I should say this. I gave half the evidence. The other half of the evidence was silent on this question. Mr. Rosen makes no reference to the activities of breaking and entering or pushing their way in; no reference to quietening anybody down; no reference to threatening to break down the door if the lady would not come out of the bathroom; no reference to the individual starting to yell at him. I think it should have been ascertained why there is this conflict in evidence unless we are to assume that perhaps the feeling in the other place-

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, it is quite true, as the hon. member says, this witness did not say anything about forcing his way into the room, but neither did he say whether he had a hair cut, a shave or had on a clean shirt. This has nothing to do with the evidence, Mr. Chairman. My submission is that this sort of discussion could go on ad infinitum. It adds nothing to the case. We must deal with the evidence as it appears in the record.
Very sound.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There is one point that perhaps should be brought out. The hon. member has been discussing at some length the question of forcing entrance, and that sort of thing. It is quite true that he can refer to how they got in there but the method by which they got in has nothing to do with this committee. I think this is under the jurisdiction of other departments of the municipal government. It is quite true the hon. member can refer to how they go in there but to go farther than that has no bearing on this bill.

I agree with you, Mr. Chairman, that their method of entry has nothing to do with whether adultery took place or not. This is the key point in the bill.
I would submit what they discovered once they made entry had nothing to do with whether or not adultery had been committed. This was another factor which the hon. member for Timiskaming developed in connection with this bill, and which I think requires a bit of additional discussion.
Perhaps I should say, as a sort of tardy defence, Mr. Chairman, that I only made reference to this question of forcible entry as it may relate to the rights of individual

citizens under the Criminal Code, and that we should not countenance this sort of thing to the slightest degree.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order; the Chair suggested to the hon. member that he had gone into this question in greater detail than was necessary. I do not see that there is any reason now to repeat it.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, but as I said, this is only in tardy defence of my action and I had just reached the end of that reference, in any event. I was going to get to the question of adultery. At one time I thought I understood the meaning of adultery. I had read about it and seen references to it in the newspapers and things of that nature. I had had discussions with other people, as one does from time to time, about this sort of thing. I thought I understood just what it did mean. However, in participating in these debates, and after listening to some conversations here, quite frankly I have come to the conclusion I do not know what it is. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, some guidance is needed from you, and I am sure you will not hesitate to provide it, if I am off the track a bit. Perhaps some guidance is needed as to what the rules are in this committee, in connection with the passage of this particular bill, in relation to what adultery means. What do we take it to mean?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order; this question was discussed, I believe last Tuesday, and the Chair ruled that a definition of adultery had nothing to do with this bill. The committee of the other place apparently has decided that adultery has been committed. Hon. members of the committee can suggest that they believe it has or that it has not, and vote one way or the other. This is their privilege. They do not have to agree with the committee of the other place, but the Chair will not allow the discussion of a definition of adultery at this time.

Then may I say, from the outset, that I disagree with the other place entirely in the conclusion to which the other place has come. I say that, not in criticism of the other place in any way but only to indicate that I disagree with the committee of the other place on this point. If I cannot engage in a discussion of my thoughts as to what adultery does mean, perhaps I might be permitted to make reference to the evidence in this regard which seeks to establish this particular point, and thus point out why I disagree with the conclusion of the committee of the other place as to what the evidence shows. Perhaps in this way I can get my thoughts over to the committee.

Alter this Mr. Rosen had gained entry to the room, after he had knocked upon the door-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, is it permissible for an hon. member to read in this house the proceedings in the Senate with respect to this case?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It has been ruled that it is permitted to refer in this committee to the evidence given on a bill before the committee of the other place.

The evidence produced in support of adultery is given first by Mr. Rosen. I assume that we cannot get to the point of determining whether or not adultery is proved until he actually gets into the premises. There is some doubt about that in some cases. In any event, he says this:
He admitted that it was his picture, that he was-
Then he gives the name of the respondent. I do not believe that is an admission of adultery, an admission that is a picture of yourself and that you are a certain person.
He wanted to know what it was all about.
I do not take that as an admission of adultery.
I told him we were acting on behalf of his wife.
In my opinion, this is not proof of or an admission of adultery.
We looked around, it is one large room, a continental bed there, with two pillows on it, and the bed was disarranged, but we did not see anybody else.
This is not proof of adultery but is only proof of the fact that they saw one person in the apartment, that there was a continental bed with two pillows on it and the bed was disarranged.
So I asked him, "where is the woman you came into the apartment with?"
We might be getting close now in the matter of proof of adultery, but still that question itself does not prove it.
He said, "what do you need her for?" I said, "we want to speak to her."
This is not proof of adultery.
So, we tried the door which was a bathroom door, and it was locked,
Then subsequently evidence was given, Mr. Chairman, that there was a lady inside the room, and presumably she needed a slip to wear before she could come out. This is not proof of adultery, in fact it is the converse because she was in the bathroom, the man was in the bedroom and the door between them was locked. Then he goes

on to threaten her about coming out and he mentions the man's name who spoke to her through the door.
-and she asked him to give her something. He handed her something, I think it was a slip, through the bathroom door, and she opened up and came out a few minutes later dressed in a slip;
This is not proof of adultery, it is only proof that the young lady put on a slip and came out of the bathroom.
-and I asked her for her name and address, and she at first didn't want to but I told her I would check it and find out where she lived, and she told me then that her name was-
Then he gives her name and address. This is not proof of adultery. There is no indication of it. Then these questions are asked:
Q. Did you notice any clothing around the room?
A. Yes, women's clothing on the chair near the bed, and some man's underclothing and a shirt and tie on another chair in the room.
This is not proof of adultery, but is merely proof of the fact that there is clothing on a chair near the bed. If ever there was a leading question to elicit a certain answer, this is it-
